These studies usually compare agents with published entries trained under each entry’s own protocol. Simulated
agent evaluations, ours included, commonly pause the simulator while the model computes, which hides its
real-time cost [61], and frontier models controlling physical arms directly are not yet precise or efficient enough
to finish tasks within a practical action budget [62]. SO-101 Bench compares agents and learned policies on the
same episodes after training every learned policy on the same data and compute, ablates harness and model
separately, and runs the agent on the real robot.

Manipulation benchmarks and evaluation practice.  Simulated benchmarks for generalist policies [12, 13,
14, 53, 63] face saturation and train–test overlap. LIBERO instruction conditioning largely selects among
memorized tasks [16]; policies above 90% there fall below 30%, or to zero, under modest perturbations [64, 65];
and an audit of five suites finds shortcut solvability, state-of-the-art gains not established as statistically significant,
creeping overfitting and dependence on the training-data source [25]. Responses include generalization suites [66,
63], capability suites for memory of occluded objects [67] and spatial grounding [10]. Real-world evaluation
has moved to distributed pairwise comparison [68], autonomous evaluation cells [69], and statistical methods
that separate policies with few trials [11, 70]. SO-101 Bench adopts several of these lessons: it separates unseen
instances from unseen classes and keeps part of the latter private, fine-tunes every policy on the same seen-object
data under one compute budget, selects checkpoints on a separate validation set, and reports confidence intervals
over 916 episodes. It also scores two spatial skills that, to our knowledge, few benchmarks test in closed loop:

3  SO-101 Bench

SO-101 Bench evaluates language-conditioned tabletop manipulation with a single SO-101 arm [1].  It is
designed to test whether a policy can turn semantic understanding into precise physical execution: identifying
the right object among distractors, grasping objects of unfamiliar geometry, and placing them under (often
precise) spatial constraints. Every component below is shared by all evaluated policies.


3.1 Tasks

The benchmark comprises four language-conditioned tasks (Fig. 2), scored as five task families.

       • Place each object in the plastic bin. The pure grasping task: the policy must identify, grasp, transport
       and deposit every object on the table. The bin moves between episodes. We evaluate a 1-object and a
        4-object condition as separate families.

       • Place [object 1] next to [object 2]. The policy must place the target close to a referent without
        disturbing other objects, adding semantic grounding and basic spatial placement.

       • Place [object 1] between [object 2] and [object 3]. The target must end centred between two referents,
       which makes the task sensitive to object extent, orientation and fine placement; it is the most demanding
         task.

       • Move [object 1] [direction]. The policy must push or carry the target along a straight path in a
      commanded direction until it reaches the boundary formed by the next object in its way.

The bin task stresses grounding, grasp strategy and grasp precision; the three spatial tasks additionally require
relational grounding, spatial reasoning, fine-grained placement and robustness to partial occlusion. To keep
language grounding nontrivial, distractors of the same class or colour are included so that class identity alone is
insufficient, and colour words are omitted from instructions unless necessary (i.e when two objects of the same
class are on the table).

3.2  Objects and Generalization Splits

The benchmark uses 138 household objects in three generalization splits (Fig. 3): seen (48 objects that appear in
training), unseen object, seen class (43 objects whose class, e.g. bowl or pen, appears in training but whose
instance does not), and unseen class (47 objects of entirely novel classes). The splits separate transfer across

teleoperation to be graspable by the SO-101, so that failures reflect the policy rather than the hardware. Of the
unseen-class objects, 37 are kept private to prevent test-set leakage.

All objects were created using the image-to-3D tools in 3D AI Studio [71]. The ∼60 physical objects were
reconstructed from photographs of the real items and their simulated appearance and physical properties were
tuned to match them; the remaining objects were generated from internet or AI-generated images and passed
through the same pipeline (Appendix E). All simulated objects are rigid bodies.


3.3  Digital Twin

All evaluation runs in a digital twin of the original real-world setup, built in Isaac Lab [26] from a scan of the
room and the object assets of Sec. 3.2. Physics runs at 240 Hz and the policy acts at 30 Hz. Policies observe
an overhead camera and a wrist camera, both at 640 × 480, and the arm’s joint positions. The twin includes
22 background environments: 18 are used in training and in the varied evaluation episodes, and 4 are held out
(Appendix F). The robot is rendered in one of 6 training colours or one of 4 held-out colours. The real arm’s
joint calibration is aligned to the simulated kinematics so that the same policy weights can run in both domains
(Sec. 5).


3.4  Scoring

Episodes are scored automatically from simulator state. Positions are measured in the tabletop plane from where
objects rest at the start of the episode. A success condition must hold continuously for 5 s; a failure condition
ends the episode once it has held for 5 s, so briefly undoing a mistake is allowed. The robot is considered to
touch an object when any link presses on it with more than 0.05 N. Episodes time out after 30 s (75 s for 4-object
bins).

       • Bin: every object ends with its reference point (the centre of its top-down bounding box) inside the
         bin’s footprint and untouched by the robot. Fails if the bin moves more than 0.5 in.

poor arrangement cannot make success impossible. About half the episodes use the canonical appearance and

                                            84  Real-Only vs. Sim-Only Policy Correspondence

Before measuring sim2real transfer (Sec. 5), we ask a coarser question: does the digital twin reproduce the
difficulty structure of the real benchmark? If a policy trained in simulation and evaluated in the twin finds the
same tasks, splits and failure modes hard as a policy trained and evaluated in the real world, the twin is a useful
proxy for real-world evaluation even before any weights cross domains.

Setup. We fine-tune two GR00T N1.6-3B policies [72, 74] independently: a real-only policy on real tele-
operated demonstrations (so101_bench_real), evaluated on the physical SO-101, and a sim-only policy on
demonstrations collected in the digital twin (a subset of so101_bench_sim containing 3D scanned objects
from so101_bench_real, with 50% of the data volume of so101_bench_real), evaluated in simulation. We
compare them on 906 episodes matched across domains by task, instruction, ordered object set and object split.
Object poses are not identical across domains, so individual episodes are not exact replicas; the primary com-
parison is therefore at the level of the 15 task × split conditions and of failure composition, with episode-level
agreement reported as a secondary measure. Real-world outcomes and failure types were labelled by hand;
simulated failures were labelled the same way and both were mapped to three categories, semantic (wrong object
or referent(s)), grasping (grasp, lift or release failed) and placement (correct object handled, imprecise/incorrect
placement).

Difficulty is preserved across conditions.  The sim-only policy succeeds on 45% (409/906) of episodes and
the real-only policy on 61% (552/906), a gap of −15.8 pp (95% CI [−19.9, −11.8]). Despite this offset, the two
systems order the 15 conditions similarly: Pearson r = 0.86 [0.71, 0.91] and Spearman ρ = 0.74 [0.52, 0.91]
across cells (Fig. 5a). In both domains success is highest on the 1-object bin and seen objects and falls with task
difficulty and object novelty, with the 4-object bin and the between task hardest on unseen classes.

Failure modes are preserved.  The composition of failures on the spatial tasks follows the same trend in
both domains (Fig. 5b). On seen objects most failures are placement errors (69% real, 62% sim; total variation
distance 0.07); on unseen classes most are semantic or grasping errors (74% real, 93% sim). Across all splits the
two failure mixes differ by a total variation distance of 0.13. On the 4-object bin, the real-only policy bins 67%
of objects and the sim-only policy 47%; per-episode progress is weakly correlated across domains, likely due to
the small size of the sim dataset for this experiments (Spearman ρ = 0.35; Fig. 5c).

Episode-level agreement is moderate.  Paired episodes have the same outcome 66% of the time (MCC 0.36),
and where both failed the failure type matches in 47% of cases (Cohen’s κ = 0.17). This is expected given
differeing training dataset scales, initial poses and stochastic policies, and is why we emphasize condition-level
correspondence. Full results are in Appendix A.

Overall, because the two policies differ in training data as well as in evaluation domain, this experiment cannot
attribute the absolute gap to the simulator; the lower sim success reflects both policies and domains together.
What it does show is that the twin reproduces which conditions are hard and why policies fail there. Section 5
isolates the simulator by running identical weights (with sim training only) in both domains.


5  Sim2Real with No Real Data

A simulated benchmark is only useful if it tells us which policies are better in the real world. We test this
directly: five policies that never saw real data from our setup are evaluated, with identical weights, both in the
digital twin and on the physical SO-101.

Abstract
The article describes the measurement of unidirectional pose accuracy and repeatability of a collaborative robot. The
objective of the measurements is to investigate and evaluate unidirectional accuracy of the six-axis collaborative robot
UR5 of the company Universal Robots. The measurement methodology was based on outlining an imaginary ISO cube
placed in the robot’s workspace, in which the robot’s tool centre point (TCP) attained five measurement points in thirty
measurement cycles. A video camera and six linear incremental sensors with six evaluation units were used for the mea-
surement. The measured values are presented and applied according to the ISO 9283 standard. On the basis of the mea-
surement, we verified technical specifications of unidirectional pose accuracy and repeatability of the robotic arm UR5
specified by its producer.


Keywords
Unidirectional pose accuracy, unidirectional pose repeatability, measuring cube, collaborative robot UR5, programming
and simulation

                                                  Abstract[cs.RO]                   Recent advances in robotics and autonomous systems have broadened the use
                              of robots in laboratory settings, including automated synthesis, scalable reac-

                         paper presents a comprehensive development of a mobile manipulator designed to
                               assist human operators in such autonomous lab environments. Kinematic mod-
                              eling of the manipulator is carried out based on the Denavit–Hartenberg (DH)
                          convention and inverse kinematics solution is determined to enable precise and
                          adaptive manipulation capabilities. A key focus of this research is enhancing the
                          manipulator’s ability to reliably grasp textured objects as a critical component of
                       autonomous handling tasks. Advanced vision-based algorithms are implemented
                           to perform real-time object detection and pose estimation, guiding the manip-
                            ulator in dynamic grasping and following tasks. In this work, we integrate a
                             vision method that combines feature-based detection with homography-driven
                         pose estimation, leveraging depth information to represent an object’s pose as
                        a 2D planar projection within 3D space. This adaptive capability enables the

1 Introduction

Autonomous robotic systems are reshaping research workflows by enabling scalable,
efficient, and safe operations in laboratory environments [1]. Within this shift, manipu-
lators mounted on mobile platforms [2], [3] have emerged as dynamic agents capable of
performing tasks like sample transport, equipment handling, and autonomous exper-
imentation. A cornerstone of these capabilities lies in reliable object tracking and
grasping, particularly when dealing with fragile or hazardous materials. To perform
these tasks with precision, vision-based object detection and pose estimation have
become central tools in robotics, allowing for real-time perception and adaptive motion
planning. Leveraging color and depth information, robots in self-driving laboratories
can interact with diverse objects, adjusting dynamically to changes in shape, texture,
and environmental conditions.
   While recent innovations have expanded the reach of autonomous systems, deploy-
ing robust grasping in unstructured lab environments remains challenging. Factors
like lighting variability, occlusion, and clutter introduce complexity to object recogni-
tion and manipulation. Overcoming these challenges requires a synergistic framework
that combines mechanical modeling, control stability, and perceptual accuracy. In
this work, we propose a comprehensive system that integrates kinematic model of a
manipulator with real-time perception to enhance grasping reliability in self-driving
chemical laboratories. The mobile manipulator is developed to follow and grasp tex-
tured objects, supporting autonomous workflows and minimizing human intervention.
Major contributions of this paper are as follows:

• Complete system integration: Developed a kinematic analysis framework for a
  mobile manipulator tailored to autonomous chemical laboratories, enabling seam-
   less integration into self-driving lab infrastructure through coordinated control and
  perception modules.
• Simulation and Real-World Performance Assessment  : Validated system
  performance via simulation and real-world experiments, reporting quantitative met-
   rics such as pose estimation error and grasping success rate to demonstrate feasibility
  and reliability.

   Despite substantial progress, object identification and pose recovery remain chal-
lenging in real-world laboratory environments due to variability in object shape,
texture, and appearance. These challenges are further exacerbated by occlusions, clut-
tered scenes, inconsistent lighting, and background interference, all of which degrade
the reliability of recognition algorithms. To address these issues, we updated a vision
pipeline [4] that integrates feature-based detection with homography-driven pose esti-
mation, augmented by depth sensing. This method enables robust 2D planar projection
of objects within 3D space, allowing the mobile manipulator to adapt to dynamic ori-
entations and environmental conditions. By balancing precision with computational


                                     2efficiency, the system supports real-time manipulation tasks essential for autonomous
experimentation and human-robot collaboration in self-driving laboratories.
   In this work, we integrate our methodology within a self-driving laboratory setup,
where autonomous robotic systems continuously operate without human intervention,
leveraging real-time object detection and pose estimation techniques. The self-driving
laboratory provides a dynamic environment for validating adaptability and precision
in robotic grasping tasks, ensuring that robots can efficiently navigate, recognize, and
manipulate objects under varied conditions. By utilizing RGB and depth data within
this automated setting, we enhance robotic perception and interaction to follow a
textured object and facilitating reliable grasping.

2 Background

Object detection has evolved significantly over the past two decades as shown in
Table 1, transitioning from handcrafted feature-based methods to deep learning-driven
architectures. Early approaches relied heavily on sliding window techniques and fea-
ture descriptors. One of the foundational methods was the Viola-Jones detector [5],
which used Haar-like features and an AdaBoost classifier for real-time face detec-
tion. Although efficient, its applicability was limited to rigid objects and constrained
environments. The introduction of Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) by Dalal
and Triggs [6] marked a major advancement in dynamic object detection. HOG fea-
tures, combined with Support Vector Machines (SVM), provided robust performance
in detecting dynamic objects in varied poses and lighting conditions. However, these
traditional methods struggled with scale variation and complex backgrounds.
  A paradigm shift occurred with the advent of deep learning. Girshick et al. [7] pro-
posed R-CNN (Regions with Convolutional Neural Networks), which combined region
proposals with CNN-based classification. Despite its accuracy, R-CNN was compu-
tationally expensive due to its multi-stage pipeline. To address this, Fast R-CNN
[8] and Faster R-CNN [9] introduced architectural refinements, including the Region
Proposal Network (RPN), significantly improving speed and efficiency. Single-stage
detectors emerged to further enhance real-time performance. Redmon et al. [10] intro-
duced YOLO (You Only Look Once) in 2016, which reframed object detection as a
regression problem. YOLO’s unified architecture enabled real-time detection but ini-
tially suffered from localization errors. Successive versions like YOLOv2, YOLOv3, and
YOLOv4 improved accuracy and robustness, while YOLOv5 and YOLOv7 incorpo-
rated advanced backbone networks and data augmentation strategies. Simultaneously,
Liu et al. [11] proposed SSD (Single Shot MultiBox Detector), which used multi-scale
feature maps for de

YOLOv4 improved accuracy and robustness, while YOLOv5 and YOLOv7 incorpo-
rated advanced backbone networks and data augmentation strategies. Simultaneously,
Liu et al. [11] proposed SSD (Single Shot MultiBox Detector), which used multi-scale
feature maps for detecting objects of varying sizes. RetinaNet [12] tackled the class
imbalance problem using Focal Loss, achieving high accuracy on challenging datasets
like COCO.
   Transformer-based models have recently gained traction. Carion et al. [13] intro-
duced a novel end-to-end detection framework named ’DETR’ using transformers for
object localization and classification. Although the method simplified the pipeline, its
convergence time was a concern. Subsequent models like Deformable DETR and DINO
refined the architecture for faster training and improved performance. Despite these



                                     3advancements, several challenges persist. Small object detection, occlusion handling,
and domain adaptation remain active research areas. Context-aware models [14] and
zero-shot detection frameworks are being explored to address these limitations. More-
over, real-time deployment on edge devices demands lightweight models like YOLOv10
[15] which optimize both accuracy and latency.
   SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) [16] is a robust computer vision tech-
nique used for detecting and describing local features in images. It enables reliable
object recognition by extracting keypoints that are invariant to scale, rotation, and
partial affine transformations, making it highly effective in dynamic or cluttered envi-
ronments. These features are matched across images using descriptor-based indexing
methods, allowing for precise localization and identification of objects. Vaithiyanathan
et al. [17] presented a real-time object recognition system that leveraged SIFT-based
local image features, which are resilient to rotation, scaling, translation, and partial
illumination changes. Keypoints are extracted using phased filtering in scale space
and matched via nearest-neighbor search to determine object presence. Recognition
results, based on descriptor count thresholds, are displayed on a microcontroller-driven
output unit.
   Object pose estimation [18] refers to the process of determining the position and
orientation of an object in a given coordinate frame, typically in 3D space. It plays
a critical role in robotics, augmented reality, and computer vision applications where
spatial understanding is essential. Pose estimation algorithms often rely on visual
cues such as keypoints, contours, or depth data to infer the object’s six degrees of
freedom (translation along x, y, z axes and rotation around them). Techniques range
from classical methods like Perspective-n-Point (PnP) and template matching to deep
learning-based approaches that regress pose directly from image features. Accurate
pose estimation enables tasks like grasping, navigation, and interaction with objects in
dynamic environments. Object pose estimation is a cornerstone of intelligent robotic
perception, enabling machines to understand and interact with their environment in
a spatially aware manner. By accurately determining an object’s position and ori-
entation, robots can perform tasks such as grasping, manipulation, navigation, and
assembly with precision and reliability [19]. This capability is especially critical in
dynamic or unstructured settings like warehouses, homes, or surgical environments
where real-time decision-making depends on spatial context. Pose estimation also
facilitates seamless integration between vision and control systems, allowing robots
to adapt to changing conditions, avoid collisions, and execute complex motions. Ulti-
mately, it transforms raw sensory data into actionable intelligence, bridging perception
and action in autonomous systems.
  Wang et al. [20] presented DenseFusion, a real-time framework for 6D object pose
estimation from RGB-D images. The method introduced a heterogeneous architec-
ture that processed RGB and depth data separately, then fused them using a dense
pixel-wise feature embedding network to estimate object poses. By integrating an end-
to-end iterative refinement module, DenseFusion significantly improved pose accuracy
in cluttered scenes and demonstrates strong performance on benchmark datasets and
real-world robotic manipulation tasks. Xiang et al. [21] proposed PoseCNN, a convolu-
tional neural network designed for 6D object pose estimation using RGB images. The



                                     4method estimated 3D translation by localizing object centers and predicting depth,
while 3D rotation is regressed via quaternion representation, with a novel loss function
to handle symmetric objects. PoseCNN demonstrated strong robustness to occlusion
and achieves state-of-the-art results on the OccludedLINEMOD dataset, supported
by the introduction of the large-scale YCB-Video dataset for benchmarking.
   The rapid advancement of object detection and pose estimation has not only revolu-
tionized visual perception systems but also significantly empowered robotic platforms,
particularly mobile manipulators. These systems rely on robust and real-time object
detection to perceive, localize, and interact with their surroundings in dynamic and
unstructured environments. Mobile manipulators that integrate a versatile robotic arm
with a mobile base have become indispensable in a range of domains such as industrial
automation, logistics, and healthcare. These integrated platforms combine mobility
with dexterous manipulation, enabling them to perform complex tasks in dynamic
environments. Their emerging role in chemistry laboratories presents unique challenges
and opportunities, especially given the sensitive and often hazardous nature of chem-
ical substances. Tasks such as transferring fragile glassware, dispensing reagents, or
interacting with laboratory equipment demand exceptional precision and reliability.
   Despite the growing interest in automating laboratory workflows, deploying mobile
manipulators and fixed base manipulators [22], [23] in chemical and pharmaceuti-
cal environments presents several persistent challenges including precision handling,
infrastructure variability, and safety in hazardous conditions. Recent studies have
begun addressing these gaps through targeted innovations. Angelopoulos et al. [24]
tackled the challenge of high-precision sample injections by developing a mobile manip-
ulation framework that combines deep learning-based syringe localization with visual
servoing, achieving millimeter-scale accuracy in gas chromatograph interactions. While
robust to navigation and grasping uncertainties, the study acknowledged limitations in
generalizing across diverse lab setups, pointing to future work in multi-modal sensing
and broader task automation.
   Fizet et al. [25] and JAG Robotics [26] addressed logistical inefficiencies by deploy-
ing mobile manipulators equipped with vision systems and temperature-controlled
storage for inter- and intra-laboratory transport. Their work improved traceability and
operational throughput, yet highlighted the difficulty of integrating robots across het-
erogeneous lab infrastructures underscoring the need for standardized interfaces and
coordinated fleet management. In hazardous environments, the importance of task-
specific end-of-arm tooling (EOAT) was emphasized by [27], which identified a gap in
adaptive control systems capable of handling varied chemical containers and environ-
mental constraints. CRL Solutions [28] contributed to safety in radiopharmaceutical
production through telemanipulators for remote vial handling, but noted limitations
in automation scalability and integration with modern robotic platforms.
    Industrial manipulators such as those from PS Lift [29] and Dalmec NA [30] have
improved ergonomic material handling in chemical manufacturing. However, their
static and task-specific nature limits adaptability, suggesting future research into mod-

explored simulated deployment using ROS2 and MoveIt2 for autonomous navigation
and manipulation within lab settings. While promising, the study emphasized the need

3 Methodology

We have carried out kinematic modeling and performed workspace analysis to
determine the feasible interaction zone. Inverse kinematic solutions obtained using
kinematic equations are applied to compute joint configurations that allowed the sys-
tem to follow the object’s trajectory to reach object pose with precision, facilitating
reliable grasping and manipulation. We employed a planar pose estimation algorithm
for tracking a textured object and later the determined pose information is used for
planning trajectory. Initially, the process begins with feature extraction and template
matching, ensuring robust identification of key object characteristics. This is followed
by homography estimation and perspective transformation, which allow for accurate
spatial mapping and alignment. Subsequently, directional vectors are estimated on the
object surface to facilitate precise orientation analysis. Finally, planar pose estimation
is performed utilizing depth data, enabling reliable grasping and interaction.
   The object detection approach started by extracting distinctive features using SIFT
from images of planar objects and matching them with features detected in images


                                     6captured by the camera. These features, such as edges, corners, blobs, and ridges,
serve as key patterns for describing the image content. Following feature extraction,
the presence of an object is ascertained by evaluating the correspondence between
extracted features and those of a reference image associated with the target object. To
mitigate the issue with high computational cost, we employed the FLANN implemen-
tation [32] of K-d Nearest Neighbor Search, optimizing matching for high-dimensional
features. To estimate the homography, we used matches obtained from the nearest
neighbor search as input. However, some of these matches can be incorrect, leading to
false correspondences that hinder accurate homography estimation. To address this, we
employed RANSAC [33], which robustly estimated homography by selecting only inlier
matches. Unlike conventional approaches that process large datasets before attempt-
ing to eliminate outliers often require substantial computational resources and risking
model distortion, RANSAC adopts a more efficient strategy. It begins with a minimal,
randomly selected subset of observations and iteratively refines the model parameters
by evaluating the consistency of additional data points. Through this randomized sam-
pling and consensus-building mechanism, RANSAC effectively isolates outliers early
in the process, enabling accurate homography estimation even in the presence of noisy
or ambiguous data. This optimization enhanced both speed and accuracy, making it
well-suited for real-time applications. In this study, perspective transformation is uti-
lized to approximate corresponding points within the test image template, facilitating
the derivation of basis vectors for the object’s surface. Subsequently, depth information
is incorporated to compute the surface normal of the planar object, thereby enabling
accurate estimation of its 3D pose.





Fig. 1 Methodology adopted in this work


   The flow of different tasks carried out in this work is shown in Fig. 1. The process of
robotic manipulation begins with kinematic modeling, which involved solving inverse
kinematics and conducting workspace analysis to determine feasible configurations
for the robot’s end effector. This foundational stage ensured that the manipulator
can reach and interact with objects within its operational domain. Following this,
object detection is performed through feature extraction and matching techniques,
enabling the system to identify and localize target objects within the environment.
Once detected, pose estimation is employed to determine the precise position and
orientation of the object, providing critical spatial information for manipulation. The


                                     7final stage involved adaptive grasping, in which the robot dynamically adjusts its grasp
strategy to eliminate singular regions and ensure stable interaction with the object.
This sequential framework facilitates reliable and flexible autonomous handling in
complex and variable settings.

                                       ABSTRACT26

                              Robotics is undergoing a significant transformation powered by advances in high-
                                   level control techniques based on machine learning, giving rise to the field of robot
                                  learning. Recent progress in robot learning has been accelerated by the increas-
                               ing availability of affordable teleoperation systems, large-scale openly available
                                   datasets, and scalable learning-based methods. However, development in the field[cs.RO]                          of robot learning is often slowed by fragmented, closed-source tools designed
                                  to only address specific sub-components within the robotics stack.  In this pa-
                                    per, we present lerobot, an open-source library that integrates across the entire
                                robot learning stack, from low-level middleware communication for motor con-
                                      trols to large-scale dataset collection, storage and streaming. The library is de-
                               signed with a strong focus on real-world robotics, supporting accessible hardware
                               platforms while remaining extensible to new embodiments. It also supports effi-
                                  cient implementations for various state-of-the-art robot learning algorithms from
                                multiple prominent paradigms, as well as a generalized asynchronous inference
                                   stack. Unlike traditional pipelines which heavily rely on hand-crafted techniques,
                      lerobot emphasizes scalable learning approaches that improve directly with
                          more data and compute.  Designed for accessibility, scalability, and openness,
                      lerobot lowers the barrier to entry for researchers and practitioners to robotics
                              while providing a platform for reproducible, state-of-the-art robot learning.arXiv:2602.22818v1
                1  INTRODUCTION

                      Early successes in robotics relied on the precise description of robot-environment interactions, typi-
                         cally consisting in analytical descriptions of rigid-body kinematics, contact modeling, and planning
                     under uncertainty (explicit models). While effective in controlled settings, deriving accurate models
                         for diverse deployment scenarios is difficult and error-prone, often requiring substantial expert effort
                    and thus has limited scalability. Recent advances in Machine Learning (ML) have catalyzed a shift
                     toward tackling robotics problems with implicit models, typically learned rather than formulated.

             A key advantage of learning-based methods (implicit models) is their scalability: performance em-
                          pirically improves with larger datasets, and more compute. In turn, the shift from explicit to implicit
                    models promises to address many of the challenges holding robotics back: rather than hand-tuning
                        the different components of a typical robotics pipeline, robot learning algorithms learn monolithic

Figure 1: lerobot is an open-source library for end-to-end robot learning.  It covers the entire
stack, from middleware motor interfaces to large-scale data collection and dataset streaming, sup-
porting an optimized inference stack, scalable implementations of SOTA robot learning algorithms,
and providing support for training custom models as well as easily reusing pre-trained ones.


control policies end-to-end, adapting to different input modalities and typically improve with in-
creasing quantities of data, echoing broader trends in vision, language, and multimodal learning.

Despite this momentum, the robot learning ecosystem is fragmented as (1) high-to-low level control
interfaces (middleware) are often tailored to specific robots and difficult to adapt, and (2) datasets
lack common formats and tooling, resulting in robot and task-specific contributions that are difficult
to reproduce and use in practice. lerobot is an open-source library providing a unified, end-to-end
stack for robot learning, and it is vertically integrated across the stack featuring:

        • Unified robot integration. A consistent, Python-based middleware API for real-world
        motor control across diverse platforms, bridging typical ML frameworks and real-world
         robotics across a variety of robots, ranging from low-end manipulators to humanoid arms
       and hands.

        • Standardized datasets.  An efficient, multimodal format for recording, storing, and
        streaming high frame-rate sensory and image data via LeRobotDataset, a custom
         dataset format built for scale. With seamless integration into the open-source ecosystem,

2.2  ROBOT LEARNING

Reinforcement Learning  Reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton & Barto, 2018) has been ex-
tensively applied to robotics (Kober et al., 2013), for the inherently sequential nature of control
problems and Deep RL’s capability to learn strategies for return maximization maxπ J(π) =
maxπ Eτ∼π PTt=0 γtrt   directly from highly-dimensional, unstructured observations such as
images (Mnih  et  al., 2013).    Off-policy,  entropy-regularized methods such as Soft Actor
Critic (Haarnoja et al., 2018) can be adapted to exploit teleoperation data and safely train in the
real-world, thereby sidestepping concerns related to operative safety and simulation-induced dis-
crepancies. Reinforcement Learning with Prior Data (RLPD) (Ball et al., 2023) mixes offline and
online buffers without pretraining to speed up convergence, and in conjuction with (1) learned re-
ward classifiers overcoming the need to define brittle hand-crafted rewards (Luo et al., 2025) and
(2) targeted human interventions during training, can yield near-perfect success rates in challenging
manipulation tasks within 1-2 hours of real-world training (HIL-SERL, Luo et al. (2024)).

Imitation Learning  Imitation Learning via Behavioral Cloning (BC) offers a pragmatic alterna-
tive to real-world RL by learning control directly from human demonstrations, eliminating the need
for reward design and reducing exploration risk by learning to reproduce the behavior of an expert
demonstrator (Pomerleau, 1988). Collected via teleoperation on increasingly affordable hardware,
large corpora of robotics data also enable training at a scale across tasks and embodiments (Collab-
oration et al., 2025; Khazatsky et al., 2025). BC relies on learning generative models of the joint
(or conditional) distribution over state-action pairs p : S × A 7→[0, 1], p(a, s) (or p(a|s)) to learn
from data distributions exhibiting multiple modes, such as teleoperation data (Florence et al., 2022).
Recent works in BC thus employ powerful generative models to learn the conditional distribution
p(a|s), learning from multimodal demonstrations and produce coherent action sequences: Zhao et al.
(2023) leverages (conditional) Variational Auto-Encoders (Kingma & Welling, 2022; Sohn et al.,
2015), Chi et al. (2024) relies on Diffusion Models (Ho et al., 2020) whereas Black et al. (2024);
Shukor et al. (2025) both rely on Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2023). Inspired by successes in
developing foundation models for vision (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) and language (OpenAI, 2024),
BC is also increasingly being used in efforts aiming to develop robot foundation models (Jang et al.,
2022; Brohan et al., 2023; Black et al., 2024), scaling up both data and compute used to learn visuo-
motor policies suitable for real-world deployment across tasks and even robot embodiments.

Robot learning algorithms are often implemented as standalone components and their integration
with the rest of the robotics stack remains challenging.


2.3  PRACTICAL CHALLENGES FOR ROBOT LEARNING RESEARCH

Despite scientific advances, the robot learning ecosystem remains fragmented, impeding repro-
ducibility and raising the barrier to entry for research.

        • Disaggregated Middleware: While middleware abstractions are available, it is common
         to encounter middleware components tailored to specific platforms in practice. This het-
         erogeneity often forces teams to develop bespoke adaptations, siloing efforts.

        • Datasets and Formats: Large-scale datasets are typically shared in a different formats.
        Data is often released in varied formats like TensorFlow Datasets, ROS bags, or bespoke
      JSON layouts. The absence of a universal, modality-rich schema prevents the seamless
        aggregation of disparate datasets into larger mixtures.

        • Learning Frameworks: The deep learning literature has consistently demonstrated that
        minor implementation differences in algorithms, data handling, and evaluation pipelines
        can lead to significant variance in results (Henderson et al., 2018). In robotics, these issues
         are compounded by hardware variability, further hindering reproducibility.

This ecosystem-wide fragmentation imposes significant incidental complexity on researchers, di-
verting resources from core scientific inquiry to systems integration.  lerobotaddresses these
limitations by providing an end-to-end, open, and scalable library designed to unify hardware in-
terfacing, collecting and streaming data, and training and deploying advanced policies with minimal
engineering overhead.

4.3  Evaluation protocol and labels

Each task–policy pair targets 30 rollouts. One π0 and one π0.5 episode were removed due to incorrect
manual resets, leaving those pairs with 29. Before each rollout, an operator resets the scene and
randomises object placement within a task-speciﬁc range. Initial states are sampled independently
rather than matched across policies. v0.1 did not enforce standardised per-task wall-clock limits, so
rollout termination depended on operator judgement. The on-site operator then scores the rollout
through the control panel with a three-way quality label:

  • successful — the task goal was achieved cleanly

  • suboptimal — the goal was achieved, but with a poor-quality ﬁnish

  • failure — the goal was not achieved

The graded scheme can represent partial competence, but operators used suboptimal conserva-
tively: 89 of 2,518 policy rollouts (3.5%) carry it, so v0.1 is nearly binary. The 50 teleoperated
demonstrations per task are successful by construction and serve as training data and a human
reference.  Successful and suboptimal rollouts are trimmed at completion to remove trailing idle
frames; corrupted or unlabelled source episodes are excluded.

## 1. chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000035)

Article
Photogrammetric Characterization of Robot Positioning
Accuracy and Repeatability

Sebastián Chajón     , Jörg Reiff-Stephan *  and Norman Günther



                              iC3@Smart Production, Technical University of Applied Sciences Wildau, Hochschulring 1, 15745 Wildau,
                              Germany; sebastian.chajon@th-wildau.de (S.C.); norman.guenther@th-wildau.de (N.G.)
                                     * Correspondence: jrs@th-wildau.de


                           Abstract

                          Additive manufacturing enables the development of low-cost, self-built robotic systems;
                         however, their performance is typically not characterized by validated metrics. The pa-
                          per presents a photogrammetric concept intended for system-independent application
                              to characterize planar positioning accuracy and repeatability without access to internal
                               controller data. The method is based on a Raspberry Pi 4 camera system, image processing
                              in Python 3.12.0 and OpenCV 4.12.0, and a universal additively manufactured robot tool
                            attachment. Two position estimation strategies are investigated: a marker-based approach
                          using ArUco markers and a markerless blob-analysis method based on a ruby sphere.
                       Camera calibration is evaluated using different patterns, with a compact CharUco board
                             exhibiting the lowest RMS reprojection error (~1 px). Experimental validation follows
                             selected elements of ISO 9283:1998 and comprises 30 repetitions at five target poses for
                                linear and axial motion strategies. The results show lower positional deviations for marker-
                         based methods compared to the markerless approach, with a two-marker configuration
                            yielding the lowest mean deviation under the investigated conditions. Sub-millimeter
                            positioning accuracy and repeatability are achieved, and linear motion exhibits lower re-
                               peatability deviations than axial motion. The proposed approach provides a cost-effective
                       and flexible solution for external robot characterization, particularly suited for self-built
                       and resource-constrained systems.


                        Keywords: photogrammetry; image processing; robot characterization



                             1. Introduction

                               Additive manufacturing enables the layer-by-layer fabrication of components based

                          without reliable knowledge of their achievable accuracy, which limits the assessment of
                               their suitability for precision applications [4]. In addition, the additive manufacturing
                            process itself may influence the mechanical properties and thus the accuracy behavior of
                              robotic structures [5].
                               For the characterization of industrial robotic systems, established measurement meth-
                         ods such as SMR tracking, laser interferometry, or ball bar tests are commonly used [6,7].
                          These methods offer high measurement accuracy but require specialized metrology equip-
                       ment and substantial experimental effort. Consequently, their application to self-built
                              robotic systems, particularly in educational and cost-sensitive environments, is only feasi-
                              ble to a limited extent [8].
                               Against this background, the present work investigates a photogrammetric measure-
                       ment concept intended for system-independent application to characterize the positioning
                           accuracy and repeatability of self-built robotic systems. The approach is based on a Rasp-
                            berry Pi 4 equipped with a camera module and software solutions implemented in Python
                               3.12.0 and OpenCV 4.12.0, enabling external camera-based position estimation without
                           coupling to the robot’s internal control system [9,10].
                                Figure 1 illustrates the selected measurement setup. A universal additively manufac-
                           tured tool attachment is intended to facilitate application of the system across different
                           robot kinematics. The captured image data are used to determine the actual positions,
                        which are then compared with predefined target positions.





                              Figure 1. System overview.

                             2. Related Works

                            The characterization of robotic system accuracy has been a subject of scientific research
                                for several decades [11]. For commercial industrial robots, established and standards-based
                                  test procedures exist, in particular according to ISO 9283:1998, which defines performance
                            metrics such as positioning accuracy and repeatability and provides standardized exper-
                           imental methods for their determination [7]. In practice, these procedures are typically
                        implemented using external measurement systems and are primarily designed for indus-
                                    trial serial robot systems [8].
                                 Established measurement methods include spherical mounted retroreflectors (SMRs),
                               laser interferometry, ball bar measurement systems, and sensor-based calibration solu-
                               tions [8,12]. These methods enable very high measurement accuracy and are used in partic-
                              ular for the precise calibration of industrial robotic systems. At the same time, they require
                              substantial equipment effort and impose specific requirements on the measurement setup
                       and system integration, which limits their applicability outside industrial environments.

                                Vision-based measurement systems have been successfully applied to the experimen-
                                    tal determination of positioning accuracy and repeatability and are characterized by a high
                           degree of external applicability. Recent developments in camera-based robot characteriza-

approach strategy, 30 repetitions were performed at five predefined target positions,

                                   Intentional motion along the z-axis was programmatically excluded. All movements
                        were performed exclusively in the x–y plane at a constant tool height, ensuring that the
                         measured deviations can be attributed solely to planar positioning and repeatability effects.

                             7. Results and Discussion

                              For the conversion from pixel coordinates to metric coordinates, the known edge
                            length of the ArUco marker was used as a planar reference. After camera calibration and
                        image undistortion, an average marker size of 145.412 px was measured and assigned to
                          a real edge length of 15.0 mm, resulting in a scaling factor of 0.103 mm/px. This factor
                                    is valid for the selected measurement setup, i.e., the fixed camera position, the calibrated
                        working distance, and the approximately constant height of the marker plate within the
                         x–y measurement plane. The conversion therefore represents a planar approximation for
                            the investigated setup and is not directly transferable to different depths or altered scene
                           geometries without renewed calibration or rescaling.

                       and does not constitute a formal statistical proof of superiority.

                        The selected poses represent the center and surrounding regions of the investigated planar

                               linear motion.

                           planar implementation based on selected elements of ISO 9283:1998.
                           The results are summarized in Table 4.

                            deviations in the present setup. Since no formal significance analysis was performed,
                                this result is reported as a descriptive observation for the examined system. Both motion
                               strategies achieve positioning accuracy and repeatability in the sub-millimeter range and
                             are therefore suitable for the characterization of self-built robotic systems.

                             To contextualize these results, the datasheet of the employed UR3 robot was consulted,
                        which specifies a positioning repeatability of 0.03 mm in accordance with ISO 9283:1998.
                             In addition, an independent reference measurement was carried out using dial indicators
                      mounted to the table on which the robot was fixed. For this purpose, the robot was ap-
                          proached separately in the x- and y-directions and the corresponding positional deviations
                        were recorded using the dial indicators from both sides. The measurements resulted in a
                      mean deviation of 0.0109 mm and therefore served as an external reference for the repeata-
                                   bility of the robot itself. At the same time, this reference measurement does not represent a
                                   full validation of the complete photogrammetric measurement chain, since influences such
                             as structural vibrations, mounting conditions, and the camera-based measurement process
                             are not captured by the dial-indicator setup in the same way.
                            The repeatability deviations obtained through the photogrammetric measurement are
                           higher than the manufacturer’s specification and the independent dial-indicator reference
                         measurements. However, these results should be interpreted with caution, as they reflect
                            the combined effect of the robot’s actual positioning behavior and the uncertainty of
                            the external photogrammetric measurement chain. While the independent dial-indicator
                         measurements provide a reference for the repeatability of the robot itself, they do not fully

he repeatability deviations obtained through the photogrammetric measurement are
                           higher than the manufacturer’s specification and the independent dial-indicator reference
                         measurements. However, these results should be interpreted with caution, as they reflect
                            the combined effect of the robot’s actual positioning behavior and the uncertainty of
                            the external photogrammetric measurement chain. While the independent dial-indicator
                         measurements provide a reference for the repeatability of the robot itself, they do not fully
                                 isolate the influence of the camera-based measurement process. Factors such as calibration
                                residuals, marker detection, scale conversion, mounting conditions, and possible vibrations
                    may also contribute to the observed deviations. A strict quantitative separation between
                              robot-related and measurement-related uncertainty was not performed within the scope of
                                this study and remains an important subject for future investigations.
                             During camera calibration, a mean RMS reprojection error of 1.01 px was determined.
                         Using the planar scaling factor of 0.103 mm/px, this value indicates an error magnitude on
                            the order of approximately 0.1 mm in image space. However, the RMS reprojection error
                          should not be interpreted as a direct measure of the end-point localization uncertainty in
                            the robot workspace, since the overall measurement result is additionally influenced by
                                factors such as residual distortion, marker detection, scale conversion, mounting conditions,
                       and possible vibrations.
                                 In addition to the discussed calibration-related uncertainty, the obtained results may
                              also be influenced by further factors that were not investigated systematically in the present
                             study. These include perspective-related effects, the exact placement and geometry of
                            the markers, the stability of the illumination, assembly tolerances of the tool attachment,
                       and possible residual vibrations during image acquisition. Although care was taken to
                        keep the experimental conditions as constant as possible, the individual contribution of
                            these factors to the measured deviations was not quantified separately. Their systematic
                              investigation remains part of future work and would further improve the interpretability
                              of the measurement-chain uncertainty.
                                 Table 5 reports the mean measured coordinate values for the investigated target poses
                            together with the associated 95% confidence intervals. The values are listed according to
                            the evaluated motion strategy.

                           The accuracy characterization of robotic systems can be performed using various
                        measurement techniques, including spherical mounted retroreflector (SMR) tracking, laser
                             interferometry, telescopic ball bar systems, and photogrammetric approaches. Although
                           conventional methods provide very high measurement accuracy, they typically require
                             specialized hardware and substantial cost and are primarily intended for industrial serial
                            robot systems. As a result, their applicability is limited for small workspaces and for self-
                                built or educational robotic systems. The present work is therefore not intended as a direct
                          performance replacement for such high-precision industrial metrology methods, but rather
                            as a low-cost and accessible alternative for application-oriented robot characterization
                        where such equipment is not available.
                                 In this work, photogrammetry was investigated as a cost-effective and externally
                            applied approach for characterizing positioning accuracy and repeatability. Related vision-
                         based approaches are described in the literature as flexible solutions for external robot
                             characterization [9,14]. A comparison of camera calibration procedures based on RMS
                              reprojection error indicated that compact CharUco boards can provide sufficiently accurate
                               calibration even at short working distances [10].
                             Based on the calibrated camera model, planar position estimation in the x–y plane
                      was evaluated. The comparison of marker-based ArUco configurations and a markerless
                           blob-based approach, conducted with reference to selected elements of ISO 9283:1998,
                      showed lower deviations and more stable behavior of the marker-based configuration
                        under the investigated conditions. However, robustness under image noise and partial
                            occlusion was not systematically evaluated within the scope of this study. Redundant
                        marker configurations reduce sensitivity to image noise and partial occlusion, consistent
                          with findings reported in the literature [10,13]. In contrast, the markerless approach investi-

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:

- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,

- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to systematically search for and analyze the literature on low-cost vs. industrial robot arm performance metrics for SDL applications.
