Abstract:
<jats:p>While there has been significant progress to use simulated data to learn robotic manipulation of rigid objects, applying its success to deformable objects has been hindered by the lack of both deformable object models and realistic non-rigid body simulators. In this paper, we present Real Garment Benchmark (RGBench), a comprehensive benchmark for robotic manipulation of garments. It features a diverse set of over 6000 garment mesh models, a new high-performance simulator, and a comprehensive protocol to evaluate garment simulation quality with carefully measured real garment dynamics. Our experiments demonstrate that our simulator outperforms currently available cloth simulators by a large margin, reducing simulation error by 20% while maintaining a speed of 3 times faster. We will publicly release RGBench to accelerate future research in robotic garment manipulation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p><p dir="ltr">Robotic pick-and-place tasks are becoming increasingly relevant in modern industries, ranging from warehouses and farms to fast-food operations. A key requirement across these applications is a reliable execution framework capable of operating in uncertain environments with a defined level of reliability. This thesis presents the design and implementation of a modular pick-and-place framework utilizing ROS 2 and MoveIt 2. The system decomposes the overall task into sequential modular stages to improve clarity, facilitate debugging, and provide a foundation for future fault-tolerant extensions. Experimental validation was conducted using the AgileX PiPER robotic arm under controlled conditions. Test cases included standard pick-and-place operations, grasp failure scenarios, and motion planning failure scenarios. Results demonstrated that the system is capable of successfully completing pick-and-place tasks while recovering from common failure cases. Although the current system relies on simplified inputs and scenarios, the developed framework is intended to serve as a foundation for future fault-tolerant robotic manipulation systems.</p></jats:p>

Abstract:
A fundamental requirement for real-world robotic deployment is the ability to understand and respond to natural language instructions. Existing language-conditioned manipulation tasks typically assume that instructions are perfectly aligned with the environment. This assumption limits robustness and generalization in realistic scenarios where instructions may be ambiguous, irrelevant, or infeasible. To address this problem, we introduce RAtional MAnipulation (RAMA), a new benchmark that challenges models with both unseen executable instructions and defective ones that should be rejected. In RAMA, we construct a dataset with over 14,000 samples, including diverse defective instructions spanning six dimensions: visual, physical, semantic, motion, safety, and out-of-context. We further propose the Rational Vision-Language-Action model (RationalVLA). It is a dual system for robotic arms that integrates the high-level vision-language model with the low-level manipulation policy by introducing learnable latent space embeddings. This design enables RationalVLA to reason over instructions, reject infeasible commands, and execute manipulation effectively. Experiments demonstrate that RationalVLA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on RAMA by a 14.5% higher success rate and 0.94 average task length, while maintaining competitive performance on standard manipulation tasks. Real-world trials further validate its effectiveness and robustness in practical applications. Our project page is https://irpn-eai.github.io/RationalVLA.

Abstract:
Vision-language models (VLMs) pretrained on large-scale multimodal datasets encode rich visual and linguistic knowledge, making them a strong foundation for robotics. Rather than training robotic policies from scratch, recent approaches adapt VLMs into vision-language-action (VLA) models that enable natural language-driven perception and control. However, existing VLAs are typically massive--often with billions of parameters--leading to high training costs and limited real-world deployability. Moreover, they rely on academic and industrial datasets, overlooking the growing availability of community-collected data from affordable robotic platforms. In this work, we present SmolVLA, a small, efficient, and community-driven VLA that drastically reduces both training and inference costs, while retaining competitive performance. SmolVLA is designed to be trained on a single GPU and deployed on consumer-grade GPUs or even CPUs. To further improve responsiveness, we introduce an asynchronous inference stack decoupling perception and action prediction from action execution, allowing higher control rates with chunked action generation. Despite its compact size, SmolVLA achieves performance comparable to VLAs that are 10x larger. We evaluate SmolVLA on a range of both simulated as well as real-world robotic benchmarks and release all code, pretrained models, and training data.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The period from 2023-2025 has witnessed unprecedented advancement in AI robotics, fundamentally driven by open source collaboration that democratizes access to cutting-edge technology and enables community-scale innovation. This comprehensive survey examines four critical pillars of modern robotics research and development (R&D): (1) large-scale collaborative datasets including DROID, Open X-Embodiment, and RH20T enabled by global research consortiums, (2) open source foundation models such as Physical Intelligence's Pi0, NVIDIA's Isaac GR00T N1, and community developments like RT-2 and PaLM-E, (3) open simulation platforms including Isaac Sim, MuJoCo 3.0, and specialized benchmarks, and (4) the open source ecosystem infrastructure spanning ROS 2, governance models, and sustainability frameworks. We analyze technical capabilities, practical deployment considerations, open source business models, and community-driven development strategies, providing actionable guidance for researchers, industry practitioners, and policymakers. Our analysis reveals that collaborative cross-embodiment learning achieves 50% performance improvements over single-institution approaches, while open source foundation models demonstrate democratized access to state-of-the-art capabilities previously available only to well-funded organizations. We identify critical open source infrastructure gaps including real-time safety validation frameworks, universal hardware abstraction layers, and sustainable funding models, while highlighting successful communitydriven solutions like the Open Source Robotics Alliance with $1 billion in estimated project value. The report demonstrates that open source has become essential infrastructure for robotics innovation, requiring strategic community investment and sustainable governance models for continued progress.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Standardized evaluation measures have aided in the progress of machine learning approaches in disciplines such as computer vision and machine translation. In this paper, we make the case that robotic learning would also benefit from benchmarking, and present a template for a vision-based manipulation benchmark. Our benchmark is built on “REPLAB,” a reproducible and self-contained hardware stack (robot arm, camera, and workspace) that costs about 2000 USD and occupies a cuboid of size 70x40x60 cm. Each REPLAB cell may be assembled within a few hours. Through this low-cost, compact design, REPLAB aims to drive wide participation by lowering the barrier to entry into robotics and to enable easy scaling to many robots. We envision REPLAB as a framework for reproducible research across manipulation tasks, and as a step in this direction, we define a grasping benchmark consisting of a task definition, evaluation protocol, performance measures, and a dataset of over 50,000 grasp attempts. We implement, evaluate, and analyze several previously proposed grasping approaches to establish baselines for this benchmark. ## 2. 3D gaze cursor: Continuous calibration and end-point grasp control of robotic actuators
Valid Text Names:

    year = "2016",
    journal = "2016 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)",
    pages = "3295-3300",

    doi = "10.1109/icra.2016.7487502",

Abstract:
Eye movements are closely related to motor actions, and hence can be used to infer motor intentions. Additionally, eye movements are in some cases the only means of communication and interaction with the environment for paralysed and impaired patients with severe motor deficiencies. Despite this, eye-tracking technology still has a very limited use as a human-robot control interface and its applicability is highly restricted to 2D simple tasks that operate on screen based interfaces and do not suffice for natural physical interaction with the environment. We propose that decoding the gaze position in 3D space rather than in 2D results into a much richer “spatial cursor” signal that allows users to perform everyday tasks such as grasping and moving objects via gaze-based robotic teleoperation. Eye tracking in 3D calibration is usually slow - we demonstrate here that by using a full 3D trajectory for system calibration generated by a robotic arm rather than a simple grid of discrete points, gaze calibration in the 3 dimensions can be successfully achieved in short time and with high accuracy. We perform the non-linear regression from eye-image to 3D-end point using Gaussian Process regressors, which allows us to handle uncertainty in end-point estimates gracefully. Our telerobotic system uses a multi-joint robot arm with a gripper and is integrated with our in-house “GT3D” binocular eye tracker. This prototype system has been evaluated and assessed in a test environment with 7 users, yielding gaze-estimation errors of less than 1cm in the horizontal, vertical and depth dimensions, and less than 2cm in the overall 3D Euclidean space. Users reported intuitive, low-cognitive load, control of the system right from their first trial and were straightaway able to simply look at an object and command through a wink to “grasp this” object with the robot gripper.

Abstract:
In the context of human–robot collaborative shared environments, there has been an increase in the use of optical motion capture (OMC) systems for human motion tracking. The accuracy and precision of OMC technology need to be assessed in order to ensure safe human–robot interactions, but the accuracy specifications provided by manufacturers are easily influenced by various factors affecting the measurements. This article describes a new methodology for the metrological evaluation of a human–robot collaborative environment based on optical motion capture (OMC) systems. Inspired by the ASTM E3064 test guide, and taking advantage of an existing industrial robot in the production cell, the system is evaluated for mean error, error spread, and repeatability. A detailed statistical study of the error distribution across the capture area is carried out, supported by a Mann–Whitney U-test for median comparisons. Based on the results, optimal capture areas for the use of the capture system are suggested. The results of the proposed method show that the metrological characteristics obtained are compatible and comparable in quality to other methods that do not require the intervention of an industrial robot.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Upper-limb motor impairment is a major consequence of stroke and neuromuscular disorders, imposing a sustained clinical and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Quantitative assessment of limb positioning and motion accuracy is fundamental to rehabilitation, guiding therapy evaluation and robotic assistance. The evolution of upper-limb positioning systems has progressed from optical motion capture to wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) and, more recently, to data-driven estimators integrated with rehabilitation robots. Each generation has aimed to balance spatial accuracy, portability, latency, and metrological reliability under ecological conditions. This review presents a systematic synthesis of the state of measurement uncertainty, calibration, and traceability in upper-limb rehabilitation robotics. Studies are categorised across four layers, i.e., sensing, fusion, cognitive, and metrological, according to their role in data acquisition, estimation, adaptation, and verification. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol was followed to ensure transparent identification, screening, and inclusion of relevant works. Comparative evaluation highlights how modern sensor-fusion and learning-based pipelines achieve near-optical angular accuracy while maintaining clinical usability. Persistent challenges include non-standard calibration procedures, magnetometer vulnerability, limited uncertainty propagation, and absence of unified traceability frameworks. The synthesis indicates a gradual transition toward cognitive and uncertainty-aware rehabilitation robotics in which metrology, artificial intelligence, and control co-evolve. Traceable measurement chains, explainable estimators, and energy-efficient embedded deployment emerge as essential prerequisites for regulatory and clinical translation. The review concludes that future upper-limb systems must integrate calibration transparency, quantified uncertainty, and interpretable learning to enable reproducible, patient-centred rehabilitation by 2030.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laboratory automation has transformed bioanalytical research, yet smaller research laboratories face challenges in adopting such technologies due to limited resources, time, and technical expertise, while already facing complex bioanalytical methods. To address these barriers, we developed a robotic-arm-based camera detection system featuring two software applications designed to simplify laboratory automation. Both applications use fiducial markers (Augmented Reality University of Cordoba (ArUco)), for object detection. The first application creates a 3D digital model of the robot’s environment using ArUco markers and a Python-based Open Computer Vision (OpenCV) simulated stereo vision setup, enabling automated computer-aided design (CAD) in FreeCAD. This facilitates safe and efficient robot arm navigation. The second application integrates a deep learning neural network for automated digital display recognition, achieving an in-house error rate of 1.69%, comparable to manual readings. By leveraging low-cost hardware and open-source software available on GitHub, the system is accessible to smaller research facilities, reducing programming complexity and enabling broader adoption of laboratory automation in bioanalytical workflows. This work demonstrates an affordable and effective solution for integrating robotic arms into scientific workflows, enhancing reproducibility and efficiency in bioanalytical research. Abstract:
The article aims to prove the hypothesis, that an approach direction influences repeatability at target point of a trajectory. Unlike most researches that deal with absolute accuracy, this paper is focused on determining the achievable repeatability and the influence of the direction of approach on it. To prove the hypothesis, several measurements are performed under different conditions, on industrial robot ABB IRB1200. To verify and confirm the result obtained from the resolvers located on the individual axes of the robot, the measurements are replicated using high-speed digital image correlation cameras. Using an external measuring device, the real repeatability of the robot endpoint is determined. The measurement proved the correctness of the hypothesis, i.e., the dependence of the approach direction on repeatability was proved. Furthermore, real deviations were measured and the extent of this influence on the robot repeatability was determined.

Frugal twins range from simple toy examples to low-cost surrogates of high-cost research. For example, a color-mixing self-driving laboratory (SDL) is a low-cost version of a costly multi-step chemical discovery SDL. We need frugal twins because they provide hands-on experience, a test bed for software prototyping (e.g., optimization, data infrastructure), and a low barrier to entry for democratizing SDLs. However, there is room for improvement. The true value of frugal twins can be realized in three core areas. Firstly, hardware and software modularity, secondly, purpose-built design (human-inspired vs. hardware-centric vs. human-in-the-loop), and thirdly state-of-the-art (SOTA) software (e.g., multi-fidelity optimization). We also describe the ethical benefits and risks that come with the democratization of science through frugal twins. In future work, we suggest ideas for new frugal twins, SDL educational course outcomes, and a classification scheme for autonomy levels. SDLs can be democratized by lowering their costs to increase accessibility and by creating systems that allow researchers to modify, extend, and share SDL tools to meet the needs of their science and contribute to the advancement of the SDL community. In particular, user-developed automation infrastructure is an important component of democratized SDL ecosystems. To advance community adoption of democratized SDL practices, we organized the “Democratizing Self-Driving Labs” workshop held at the 2024 Accelerate conference. As part of this workshop, the authors contributed to a demonstration of their user-developed automation infrastructure. 14 examples of custom built hardware, software, and workflows were shared. This workshop provided an opportunity for researchers to see user-developed infrastructure in action, learn about how they could integrate these projects into their work, and contribute to discussion about what is needed to advance the state of democratized SDLs. In this perspective, ten contributed examples of user-developed hardware and software from the workshop are highlighted. Despite a diverse array of projects, common motivations for pursuing user-developed infrastructure were cost savings and specification requirements that were unmet by commercially available products. Continuing to advance the state of user-developed automation infrastructure will require commitments to completing high-quality documentation for open-source hardware projects, pathways for materials researchers to learn hardware development skills, and more opportunities for researchers to share their infrastructure advancements, in addition to the scientific advancements that they enable. T.", title = "Self-Driving Laboratories: Translating Materials Science from Laboratory to Factory", year = "2025", journal = "ACS Omega", volume = "10", pages = "29902-29908", month = "Jun", doi = "10.1021/acsomega.5c02197", url = "https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c02197", publisher = "American Chemical Society (ACS)", issue = "28", issn = "2470-1343" } Abstract: The field of materials science stands at a critical inflection point. While laboratory innovations continue to emerge at an unprecedented pace, the traditional timeline from discovery to market in 10–20 years has become an unacceptable bottleneck in addressing urgent technological challenges. We argue that self-driving laboratories (SDLs) represent not merely another step in automation, but a fundamental reimagining of the materials development pipeline. By integrating manufacturing constraints and scalability considerations from the earliest stages of discovery, SDLs can collapse the laboratory-to-factory timeline while improving reproducibility and success rates. This requires abandoning the traditional sequential approach of materials screening, device optimization and manufacturing scale-up; in favor of concurrent cross-scale development. Here, we critically examine current SDL implementations, challenge prevailing assumptions about automation in materials science, and propose a roadmap for truly integrated materials development platforms that could revolutionize how we translate laboratory discoveries into commercial products. Abstract:
Autonomous laboratories can accelerate discoveries in chemical synthesis, but this requires automated measurements coupled with reliable decision-making1,2. Most autonomous laboratories involve bespoke automated equipment3–6, and reaction outcomes are often assessed using a single, hard-wired characterization technique7. Any decision-making algorithms8 must then operate using this narrow range of characterization data9,10. By contrast, manual experiments tend to draw on a wider range of instruments to characterize reaction products, and decisions are rarely taken based on one measurement alone. Here we show that a synthesis laboratory can be integrated into an autonomous laboratory by using mobile robots11–13 that operate equipment and make decisions in a human-like way. Our modular workflow combines mobile robots, an automated synthesis platform, a liquid chromatography–mass spectrometer and a benchtop nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer. This allows robots to share existing laboratory equipment with human researchers without monopolizing it or requiring extensive redesign. A heuristic decision-maker processes the orthogonal measurement data, selecting successful reactions to take forward and automatically checking the reproducibility of any screening hits. We exemplify this approach in the three areas of structural diversification chemistry, supramolecular host–guest chemistry and photochemical synthesis. This strategy is particularly suited to exploratory chemistry that can yield multiple potential products, as for supramolecular assemblies, where we also extend the method to an autonomous function assay by evaluating host–guest binding properties.

Traditional materials development pipelines typically require 10-20 years, but self-driving laboratories (SDLs) and Materials Acceleration Platforms (MAPs) aim to reduce this to 1-2 years through closed-loop systems combining physical experimentation with computational intelligence. The review analyzes critical components including robotic hardware architectures, integrated analytical instrumentation, closed-loop optimization strategies, AI-driven decision-making frameworks, and multi-agent systems for laboratory coordination. Case studies demonstrate remarkable success across various domains: nanomaterials synthesis, inorganic materials exploration, electrocatalyst discovery, and reaction mechanism elucidation. Large language models have recently enhanced these systems by improving knowledge extraction, experimental planning, and multi-agent coordination. The integration of standardized data formats, accessible materials databases, and sophisticated knowledge representation frameworks further accelerates discovery while enhancing reproducibility. This transformative paradigm represents a fundamental reimagining of materials science methodology, shifting from human-guided exploration to AI-orchestrated discovery campaigns.</jats:p>

Automated laboratory experiments have the potential to propel new discoveries, while increasing reproducibility and improving scientists' safety when handling dangerous materials. However, many automated laboratory workflows have not fully leveraged the remarkable advancements in robotics and digital lab equipment. As a result, most robotic systems used in the labs are programmed specifically for a single experiment, often relying on proprietary architectures or using unconventional hardware. In this work, we tackle this problem by proposing a novel robotic system architecture specifically designed with and for chemists, which allows the scientist to easily reconfigure their setup for new experiments. Abstract:
Lab automation has the potential to accelerate scientific progress in the natural sciences, allowing tedious experiments that would require many hours of human time to be automated, enabling higher accuracy, efficiency, and repeatability. Mobile manipulation robots have the potential to work in chemistry labs designed for humans to complete tasks for which setting up customized factory-scale automation is premature or infeasible. We present a new method to enable a mobile manipulation robot to automate injections, a common task in chemistry labs when using equipment such as gas chromatographs (GCs) for analyzing the contents of a sample mixture. This task is challenging for a mobile manipulation robot due to the need to navigate to the equipment in the lab and then achieve millimeter-scale accuracy required for the syringe positioning. Our approach leverages deep learning to create a model capable of localizing the syringe with high accuracy using cameras mounted on the chemistry equipment, and then uses a visual servoing approach based on the syringe's needle localization to achieve the injection. We demonstrate that our approach is robust to uncertainty in navigation as well as uncertainty in the grasping position and orientation of the syringe, achieving errors sufficiently small to enable the mobile manipulation robot to automate injections in real chemistry equipment.

Abstract:
Simulation has enabled unprecedented compute-scalable approaches to robot learning. However, many existing simulation frameworks typically support a narrow range of scenes/tasks and lack features critical for scaling generalizable robotics and sim2real. We introduce and open source ManiSkill3, the fastest state-visual GPU parallelized robotics simulator with contact-rich physics targeting generalizable manipulation. ManiSkill3 supports GPU parallelization of many aspects including simulation+rendering, heterogeneous simulation, pointclouds/voxels visual input, and more. Simulation with rendering on ManiSkill3 can run 10-1000x faster with 2-3x less GPU memory usage than other platforms, achieving up to 30,000+ FPS in benchmarked environments due to minimal python/pytorch overhead in the system, simulation on the GPU, and the use of the SAPIEN parallel rendering system. Tasks that used to take hours to train can now take minutes. We further provide the most comprehensive range of GPU parallelized environments/tasks spanning 12 distinct domains including but not limited to mobile manipulation for tasks such as drawing, humanoids, and dextrous manipulation in realistic scenes designed by artists or real-world digital twins. In addition, millions of demonstration frames are provided from motion planning, RL, and teleoperation. ManiSkill3 also provides a comprehensive set of baselines that span popular RL and learning-from-demonstrations algorithms.

Abstract:
We introduce ReWiND, a framework for learning robot manipulation tasks solely from language instructions without per-task demonstrations. Standard reinforcement learning (RL) and imitation learning methods require expert supervision through human-designed reward functions or demonstrations for every new task. In contrast, ReWiND starts from a small demonstration dataset to learn: (1) a data-efficient, language-conditioned reward function that labels the dataset with rewards, and (2) a language-conditioned policy pre-trained with offline RL using these rewards. Given an unseen task variation, ReWiND fine-tunes the pre-trained policy using the learned reward function, requiring minimal online interaction. We show that ReWiND's reward model generalizes effectively to unseen tasks, outperforming baselines by up to 2.4x in reward generalization and policy alignment metrics. Finally, we demonstrate that ReWiND enables sample-efficient adaptation to new tasks, beating baselines by 2x in simulation and improving real-world pretrained bimanual policies by 5x, taking a step towards scalable, real-world robot learning. See website at https://rewind-reward.github.io/.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing enables the development of low-cost, self-built robotic systems; however, their performance is typically not characterized by validated metrics. The paper presents a photogrammetric concept intended for system-independent application to characterize planar positioning accuracy and repeatability without access to internal controller data. The method is based on a Raspberry Pi 4 camera system, image processing in Python 3.12.0 and OpenCV 4.12.0, and a universal additively manufactured robot tool attachment. Two position estimation strategies are investigated: a marker-based approach using ArUco markers and a markerless blob-analysis method based on a ruby sphere. Camera calibration is evaluated using different patterns, with a compact CharUco board exhibiting the lowest RMS reprojection error (~1 px). Experimental validation follows selected elements of ISO 9283:1998 and comprises 30 repetitions at five target poses for linear and axial motion strategies. The results show lower positional deviations for marker-based methods compared to the markerless approach, with a two-marker configuration yielding the lowest mean deviation under the investigated conditions. Sub-millimeter positioning accuracy and repeatability are achieved, and linear motion exhibits lower repeatability deviations than axial motion. The proposed approach provides a cost-effective and flexible solution for external robot characterization, particularly suited for self-built and resource-constrained systems.</jats:p>

Introduction



1.1  Background


Robotic manipulation systems are becoming more and more prevalent in real-world ap-
plications where uncertainty in perception, motion planning, and execution can lead to
task failure. Ensuring reliable operation in these conditions is a key challenge, especially
for pick-and-place tasks that require close coordination between sensing, planning, and
control.

  A common method for improving robustness in robotic systems is the implementa-
tion of modular or skill-based execution frameworks, which decompose complex tasks
into smaller functional units. This modular structure improves system organization and
makes it easier to isolate and recover from failures at the level of individual tasks. While
fully fault-tolerant systems require advanced reasoning mechanisms, even partial modu-
larization can significantly improve system clarity and debugging.

   Modern robotic software frameworks such as ROS 2 (Robotic Operating System 2)
and motion planning libraries such as MoveIt 2 have allowed for the rapid development
and implementation of complex manipulation pipelines. These tools provide key capabili-
ties such as inter-process communication, simulation environments, and motion planning,
allowing development to focus on higher-level system integration.

   This thesis will present the design and implementation of a modular pick-and-place
execution framework built using ROS 2 and MoveIt 2. The system will decompose the
pick-and-place task into important sequential stages, including perception, motion plan-
ning, and execution, all run by the structured control pipeline. While the original objective
included a fully fault-tolerant skill-based architecture, the final system focuses on estab-
lishing a working modular framework that can support future fault-handling extensions.

   Experimental results will demonstrate the system’s ability to perform pick-and-place
operations under controlled conditions, highlighting both its capabilities and limitations.
This work will provide insights into practical challenges of planning systems, and will

Pick-and-place is an important robotic task because it appears in many real-world ap-
plications. Robots use pick-and-place in factories to move parts, in warehouses to sort
packages, and in other systems where objects must be moved from one location to an-

  A successful pick-and-place system must be able to locate an object, grasp it properly,
move it safely, and place it in the desired location. Because all of these steps must work
together, pick-and-place tasks are often used to evaluate the overall performance of robotic
manipulation systems [4].


                                      42.3. CHALLENGES IN ROBOTIC PICK-AND-PLACE                          5

2.3  Challenges in Robotic Pick-and-Place

Even though pick-and-place is a common task, it is still difficult for robots to perform
well in many environments. One challenge is that objects may be placed in cluttered
scenes, partially blocked, or oriented in unexpected ways. Small errors in understanding
the object or scene can lead to failed grasps or poor robot motions [3].

   Another challenge is grasp reliability. A grasp that looks correct may still fail because
of poor contact, object shape, or uncertainty in the object properties [4]. In addition, the
robot must move without colliding with the environment while still reaching the object
in a useful pose.

   Motion planning is also difficult because robotic arms usually have many joints, cre-
ating a high-dimensional planning problem. The system must find a safe and practical
path while following the robot’s limits and the task requirements [5]. These challenges
show that robotic pick-and-place is not only a grasping problem, but also a full system
problem.


2.4  Overview of Robot Grasping Methods

Robot grasping methods are usually divided into two main groups: analytical methods
and data-driven methods [4].


2.4.1  Analytical Grasping Methods

Analytical grasping methods are based on the physics and geometry of both the object
and gripper. These methods study how the robot’s end effector contacts the object and
whether the grasp can hold the object securely. These methods usually fall into 3 main
categories, frictionless contact, frictional contact, and soft-finger contact, the first two
being the most widely used [4].

   The main advantage of analytical methods is that they are easier to understand from
a mathematical point of view. However, they usually require accurate information from
their environment and rely on many simplifications. In real-world tasks, this information
is often uncertain, which makes purely analytical methods harder to use [4].


2.4.2  Data-Driven and Learning-Based Grasping Methods

Data-driven grasping methods use examples, training data, or machine learning to find
good grasps. They are broken into 3 categories, imitation-based, sampling-based, and
end-to-end learning. Instead of relying only on hand-made physical models, these meth-
ods learn which grasps are likely to succeed from previous data, removing any need for
assumptions that analytical models may rely on [4].6                            CHAPTER 2. LITERATURE REVIEW


   These methods are often more flexible when the robot must handle new or unfamiliar
objects. However, they can require large datasets, which are labour intensive, and may
not always perform well outside the conditions they were trained on [4].



2.4.3  Gripper and Hand Design

Grasping methods also depend on the type of end effector used. Common examples
include parallel-jaw grippers, suction grippers, multi-fingered hands, and soft grippers [4].
Parallel-jaw grippers are very common in industry because they are simple and reliable,
and is the type of gripper utilized in this report. More advanced grippers can perform
more complex grasps, but they are also harder to control.


2.5  Overview of Motion Planning Methods


Motion planning decides how the robot should move from its starting position to the goal
position without collisions.  In robotic manipulation, this usually means finding a safe
path for the robotic arm.



2.5.1  Sampling-Based Planning

Sampling-based planning methods are widely used in robotics. Examples include Proba-
bilistic Roadmap Method (PRM), Rapidly-expanding Random Trees (RRT), and Kinody-
namic Planning by Interior-Exterior Cell Exploration (KPIECE). These planners are able
to solve high complexity problems by sampling the working area of the robot, and then
finding the connections of the joints that work in that space through various attempts [5].

   Their main strength is that they work well in complex, high-dimensional spaces. How-
ever, the resulting path is not always smooth or optimal, and the planning result may
depend on the planner settings.



2.5.2  Optimization-Based Planning

Optimization-based planning methods treat motion planning as a mathematical optimiza-
tion problem. These methods try to improve a path while satisfying constraints such as
collision avoidance and smoothness. TrajOpt is a well-known example [6].

   These planners can produce smoother motions, and work for high DOF systems, but
they may depend strongly on the starting guess, and collision avoidance is a constant
issue [6].2.6. SOFTWARE LIBRARIES AND FRAMEWORKS FOR ROBOT CONTROL    7

communicate.

   The main advantage of ROS 2 is that it is flexible, modular, and widely used.  It

MoveIt 2 is a motion planning and manipulation tool made to work in the ROS 2 environ-

for custom hardware.

OMPL is a motion planning library that focuses mainly on sampling-based planning

3.1  System Overview



Robotic manipulation systems typically rely on a structured execution system used to
coordinate all tasks from perception, planning, and control. Common approaches to
accomplish this include state machines and behaviour trees, which decompose complex
tasks into manageable portions.  The system being developed in this paper follows a
modular pipeline that works similarly to a state machine, where each stage of the operation
performs a specific function and communicates with other components through defined
interfaces. This modular structure makes the system easier to understand and debug, and
can support more advanced fault-handling strategies in future work.

   As shown in Figure 3.1, the overall system architecture operates as a structured control
pipeline that utilizes perception, motion planning, task execution, and fault handling.
The system begins with system initialization, during which communication interfaces are
configured and turned on. The system will then wait in a loop until a pick and place pose
is specified, which will determine the target locations for the robot to move to during
operation. Once valid poses are received, the motion planner generates a collision-free
trajectory between the robot and the target poses. If no solution is found, the system will
ignore the requested poses and wait for updated poses. If a solution is found, the planned
motion will be executed using the robots controller.  During execution,  if the system
detects that a failure occurred such as invalid poses, errors in trajectory, or failures in
grasping, the robot will return to a safe predetermined position (zero position). Finally,
if the motion results in no errors, the system resets and waits for a new set of poses for
its next task.  This structured system pipeline allows for it to maintain a predictable
behaviour, while providing a basis for future implementation of more advanced methods.

3.2.3  MoveIt 2 Motion Planning

MoveIt 2 is an all-encompassing motion planning, manipulation, control, and navigation
tool made to work in the ROS 2 environment [7].  It provides tools for kinematic al-
gorithms, collision checking, motion planning, scene visualization, trajectory processing,
and even hybrid planning [7]. All of these tools allow for robotic systems to not only plan
trajectories, but to understand its environment and limits to achieve and plan realistic
tasks. Move It 2 is the most crucial component for the proposed pick-and-place system
because of its collision-free trajectory planning. Given a start and end position, MoveIt
2 is able to compute the proper joint movements using its inverse kinematics solver to
achieve said pose while avoiding any obstacles. The planner also runs through many pos-
sible solutions to complete the motion and selects the best solution given the environment
and constraints. One of the benefits of using MoveIt 2 is also its capability to generate

tasks into simpler interdependent sub tasks [13]. MTC works specifically with MoveIt 2,

the entire system and prepares the manipulation tasks into sub tasks that can be solved.
This system allows the pick-and-place task to be broken into stages such as going to the
object, grasping it, moving it to the desired location, placing, and returning to its safe
position. In figure 3.3, the proposed pipeline is illustrated.

where  if the system fails at a specific stage,  it may explore different solutions.  This
structure is important as it provides a sound foundation for future implementation of
more robust fault-handing strategies. Within this project, MTC will be used to coordinate
motion planning stages required for the pick-and-place task. The modular structure of
the task pipeline aligns with the overall system architecture, allowing individual stages to
be modified or extended without redesigning the entire execution framework.

3.3.2  Pick Sequence

Once the poses have been sent, the environment is setup with the required collision objects,
those being the desk that the arm is attached to, as well as the object that the arm is
intended to grasp and the platform it rests on. This is important because if the objects
are not generated before planning, the planner will ignore those obstacles and may lead
to collisions. The pick task is then initialized where the following stages are added.


   1. Current State


    • Makes sure that the system understands where the starting position is of the
          robot before executing any tasks


   2. Open Gripper


    • Open the gripper before moving into the object


   3. Move to Pre-Pick Pose


    • Move to a location above the object before moving down to grab it


   4. Delete Object


    • Remove the object from the scene

    • This is due to an unresolved issue where the MoveIt 2 system needs to know
          the exact width that the gripper should close at, but the realistic system can
          simply close all the way with no issue. Removing the object removes this issue
           at little loss to overall integrity of the task


   5. Move to Pick Pose


    • Move into the position sent by the camera where the gripper may grasp the
           object


   6. Close Gripper


    • Grasps the object


   Once these tasks are added, the planner is run to determine if there are any viable
trajectory’s to complete the task. If there is, the motion is executed.18                               CHAPTER 3. SYSTEM DESIGN

3.3.3  Place Sequence

If the pick task has been completed, the MTC moves to the place task, which generates
a new plan specifically for the place task. It goes as follows.


   1. Current State

    • Makes sure that the system understands where the starting position is of the
          robot before executing any tasks

   2. Move to Place Pose

    • Move the object to the location it will be left at

   3. Open Gripper

    • Let go of the object

   4. Recreate Object

    • Add the object back to the scene

    • This is done to undo the previous removal of the object, additionally, it ensures
          the arm does not collide with the object after placing.

   5. Move to Post-Place Pose

    • Move to a location above the object for a safer trajectory

   6. Return to Zero

    • Return to the zero position to wait for new commands


   Similarly to the pick task, once the stages are set, the planner is run and if a solution
is found, the motion is executed. Once the placing and return motion are completed, the
system resets again and waits for a new set of poses to complete another pick-and-place
task.


3.3.4  Fault Handling and Recovery

There are two major fault handling tasks done in this entire pipeline, confirmation of the
planner trajectory, and assessing if the gripper achieved a proper grasp.

   For the motion planner, MoveIt 2 has a built in planner check that ensures that no
faults occur during the trajectory execution. Before the system has a chance to execute,
multiple solutions to the proposed trajectory in MTC are checked for possible solutions.
If a valid path is generated, the system moves to execution and then prepares for the next3.3. PICK-AND-PLACE PIPELINE                                           19


steps. If the system ends up not generating any possible solutions, the recovery is based
on the current step.  If the planner fails in the pick stage, the system simply aborts the
sent poses and requests new ones. If the planner fails in the place stage, the system has
already been placed in the grasp position, so the system should ideally let go of the target
object and return to the zero position
   For the grasp detection, it occurs right after the pick task has been completed where
the object should already be held by the grippers. To detect if the grippers have grasped
something, the /Joint states feedback topic is utilized to detect if the the gripper joint
utilized in closing has been fully shut.  If the joint is not at zero, this indicates that an
object is not allowing it to fully close, indicating a successful grasp, moving on to the
place stage.  If the joint is fully closed, this indicates that no object is obstructing the
grasp, meaning the grasp was not successful.  If this occurs, the arm will return to the
zero position and wait for a new valid pose.Chapter 4

A computer with a high processing power is not required for this system, as the most
intensive portion of the computation is done in the MoveIt 2 program. MoveIt 2 simply
requires that the system be running on Ubuntu 22.04 which is capable of operating ROS
2 Humble, and a recommendation is to have 32 GB of RAM, but less is usable [14]. The
PiPER robotic arm does not have any specific requirements when it comes to computing
power [2]. As long as the system is setup on the proper firmware version and has the
appropriate SDK installed on the host computer, it should run as intended.


4.1.4  Workspace and Safety Constraints

For the workspace environment, important aspects to think about are what the physical
workspace layout will be, what are the limitations in the motion and reach, considerations
in what can be collided into and making proper clearance, what are the possible payload
constraints, and general operational safety measures.

   The physical workspace was limited to the elevated area of a standard classroom desk,
to which the PiPER arm was physically mounted to the center of. Due to the mobility
presented by attaching it to the desk, it was possible to move the setup to wherever was
viable, as long as a viable power source was available and all unnecessary obstructions
within the 626.75 mm working radius were removed. Any object that would be used for
the pick and place operation would be placed on another desk within sufficient range of the
arm to act as an elevated platform for where the experiment will take place. In addition,
any object used in the experiment was ensured to stay within the required constraints of
the gripper. These workspace conditions were kept constant throughout the experiments
to improve repeatability and to ensure the safety of both the operator and the equipment.

   Based on the previous section, it is important to understand the collision and clearance
considerations. When operating the arm, it should never need to go below the height of
the desk since all required objects will be at locations greater than that. Secondly, the arm
should never go near where the cables are connected to power the arm itself to prevent
any unwanted disconnections. As well, the dimensions of the objects being manipulated
should be well understood to avoid any unnecessary cases of the arm colliding with the
object, this can be handled within the MoveIt 2 software. These considerations should be
kept in mind when creating solution paths in MoveIt 2.

   As well, it is important that constraints be put on any object being worked with.
Firstly, the object should weigh considerably less than 1.5 kg which is the maximum
payload weight of the arm, and it should be able to be grasped firmly under 40 N of force
using the rubber pads of the gripper. Additionally, it is important that the object has an
area that can fit comfortably within the 70 mm maximum opening area of the gripper.
Most objects being experimented with will be similar in size to water bottles, but if an24                        CHAPTER 4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

physical workspace to ensure the picked up object does not collide with anything. If these
considerations are followed, then all unnecessary damage can be avoided.

   Operational safety measures were followed before and during each experimental run
to reduce risk to both the operator and the equipment. Before operation, the robotic arm
was checked to be securely mounted and positioned and that all power and communication
cables were connected and out of the way. Then the surrounding workspace was cleared
of unnecessary objects, and the target object was placed in a reasonable operating area.
During operation, the arm was kept in a clear visual range at all times, and the area was
kept clear from any person who may accidentally walk into the operating area.  If the
arm is in motion, the workspace is avoided by the operator until the motion is completed
to account for any unexpected or abnormal behaviour.  If an abnormality or unwanted
outcome is detected, the arm is stopped immediately and a proper check is conducted
before continuing with operation. These precautions were especially important since the
PiPER arm does not provide automatic obstacle avoidance and therefore relies on a
controlled workspace and careful supervision during operation.

      1  Introduction

        Low-cost arms have become the most common entry point to robot learning. The open-source SO-101 [1, 2] is
        a 3D-printed arm driven by six serial-bus servos; a follower arm costs about $120–150 in parts [2, 3], against
        roughly $4,900 for one ALOHA arm [4]. LeRobot [5] supports it from teleoperation to deployment, and
        SO-family arms produce most of the community robot datasets on the Hugging Face Hub.1 Open models now
          train on these data: SmolVLA was pretrained on 481 community datasets [6], and MolmoAct2 has a variant
         post-trained on 38k curated SO-100/101 episodes [7]. These models, however, are starting points for fine-tuning

          tasks, and to our knowledge no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on anarXiv:2610.36420v1

        wiping and spatial grounding; Spa-Bench tests relational placement, referential descriptions, ordinal position
        and counting, with familiar constituents in its primary evaluation and a separate novel-object pilot [10]. They

          that wore down during evaluation [3]).

spanning 1,115 real rollouts across three simulators, SIMPLER showed weak ranking agreement with the
real robot [22]. These studies also mostly run in one direction, placing policies trained on real data inside a
twin. As policies are increasingly trained on simulated data alone [23, 24], a benchmark should also show
that its ranking survives when the same sim-trained weights run on a real robot. Finally, it should measure
what aggregate success hides: a policy can complete a task without understanding it: on LIBERO, a probe that
replaces instruction text with a task-ID embedding nearly matches the best published results [25], and on a real
SO-101, VLAs that manipulate reliably can fail to adapt to OOD spatial relations [10].

We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation with a
single SO-101 arm, built so that its rankings carry over to the real robot (Fig. 1). Its core is an Isaac Lab [26]
digital twin of a real SO-101 setup with 138 household objects in three generalization splits: seen (in the
training dataset), unseen object of a seen class, and unseen class, with 37 unseen-class objects kept private.
Four tasks (place every object in a bin; place an object next to another; place it between two others; move it in
a direction until it reaches the boundary object) are scored automatically from simulator state. They require
the policy to pick out the named object among same-class distractors, grasp unfamiliar geometry and place
it under spatial constraints. The primary evaluation has 916 feasibility-checked episodes over 15 task-family
× split cells, with subsets for held-out appearances (ROBUST), rotating an object to fit a tight space (PLAN)
and remembering occluded objects (MEM). Every learned policy is fine-tuned on the same 3,629 simulated
teleoperated demonstrations of seen objects under an equal 36 h x 4 x A100 compute budget.




                                            2Two studies test whether the twin can stand in for the real robot. Independently trained real-only and sim-only
GR00T N1.6 policies find the same conditions hard (Pearson r = 0.86 across the 15 cells) and fail in the same
ways (Sec. 4). Five policies that never saw real data from our setup, four VLAs and an LLM agent, then run
with identical weights in the twin and on the physical SO-101 in an environment unseen in training, with objects
from all three splits; SO-101 Bench policies work out of the box in unseen real environments with unseen
objects. Simulation ranks them exactly as the real robot does (Spearman ρ = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000, 95% CI
[0.000, 0.169]), although it overestimates every policy’s success by 9 to 31 percentage points (Sec. 5). On the
full leaderboard of nine VLAs and WAMs, the best learned policies, InternW0-∆[27] and Galaxea 0.5 [28], are
statistically tied near 61; spatial placement and unseen classes are where they fail, and none exceeds 17% on
PLAN. The strongest entry is an LLM agent: GPT-6.1 Sol [29] writing code in the PyRUA-Lean harness [30]
and handing grasps to Galaxea 0.5 scores 83.2 and solves 75% of PLAN. Its lead comes largely from the harness.
On 60 paired episodes, Sol succeeds on 35% (21/60) with direct tool calls, 67% (40/60) with PyRUA-Lean and
85% (51/60) with the Galaxea 0.5 hand-off, against 53% (32/60) for Galaxea 0.5 alone, and the lead holds on
the real robot, 64% (29/45) against 53% (24/45).

Our contributions are:

       • SO-101 Bench, a digital-twin benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation on a low-cost
       arm, with instance- and class-level object splits, ROBUST, PLAN and MEM subsets and automatic
        scoring, released with the so101_bench_sim (3,629 simulated episodes) and so101_bench_real
       (∼4,400 real episodes) datasets.

       • Evidence that the twin ranks policies as the real robot does: condition- and failure-level correspon-
       dence between independently trained real-only and sim-only policies, and an exact sim2real ranking of
         five policies, including an LLM agent, run with identical weights and no real data from our setup; these
         policies perform language-conditioned tasks out of the box in an unseen real environment with unseen
         objects.

       • A leaderboard of nine VLAs and WAMs and two LLM agents, with every learned policy fine-tuned
       on the same data and compute, showing that spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit
        planning remain open.

       • Harness and model ablations showing that, in our setting, a code-as-policy harness that hands grasping
        to a learned policy outperforms either on their own; Direct action generation by the agent proves
        expensive and ineffective, and 6.1 Sol compares favorably to other agents.


2  Related Work

Low-cost hardware and SO-101 benchmarks.  Cheap hardware has repeatedly widened who can do robot
learning. ALOHA showed that a low-cost bimanual rig can learn fine manipulation [31], and 2026 platforms
push prices further, from a $1,688 bimanual mobile manipulator [32] to the SO-101, at about a fortieth of the
price of an ALOHA arm [4]. LeRobot [5] and community data have made the SO-100/101 a training platform
for open VLAs [6, 7]. Four 2026 benchmarks evaluate VLAs on physical SO-101 arms. Yu and Qiu [8] analyse
failure and recovery on four tasks, VLA-REPLICA is a sub-$1,100 kit reproduced across sites [9], ArmnetBench
scores 2,518 rollouts of seven policies on an arm farm [3], and Spa-Bench probes recombinations of familiar
objects, spatial concepts and actions in its primary evaluation, with a separate novel-object pilot [10]. All four
use real robot demonstrations for task-specific adaptation and evaluate on physical hardware. In simulation, the
SO-101 Task Set contains eight language-free tasks for visual reinforcement learning with sim2real transfer [15],
and LeIsaac provides SO-101 teleoperation and data-collection tooling in Isaac Lab [33]. To our knowledge,
SO-101 Bench is the first language-conditioned SO-101 benchmark with held-out object splits whose simulated
policy ranking is validated on the real arm. It also represents one of, if not the most, challenging task suites
handled by an SO-101 up to this point.

Real2sim evaluation and sim2real transfer.  Whether simulated evaluation predicts real performance was
studied early for navigation [34]; for manipulation, SIMPLER [18] showed that an aligned simulator can rank


                                            3real-world policies and introduced the MMRV metric. Twins built from scans, neural reconstructions or generated
assets now report strong score or ranking agreement within their validated settings [19, 20, 35, 36, 37, 38];
SimFoundry reaches Pearson 0.911 and MMRV 0.018 over five policy architectures [21]. Two 2026 results
temper this. Validity does not carry across setups: re-tested against new real rollouts, SIMPLER’s agreement with
the real-robot ranking is weak [22]. Reconstruction quality also matters: an authored object-and-scene pipeline
achieved sim–real correlation of 0.90 versus 0.51 for a default reconstruction in a ten-cell study [39], consistent
with our tuning of each reconstructed object against its physical counterpart (Appendix E). Learned world models
are an alternative evaluator [40], but released models often predict success on verified failures [41]. In parallel,
policies trained only on simulated data now transfer to real robots: MolmoB0T reaches 79.2% on real pick-and-
place without real demonstrations [23], OASIS pairs image-to-3D assets with teleoperation inside simulation [24],
and LEGS and Splat2Act fine-tune pretrained VLAs using only synthetic robot demonstrations [42, 43]. We
deploy five sim-trained policies, including an LLM agent, with identical weights and test whether their ranking
survives.

LLM agents for manipulation.  Language models have long planned over learned skills [44] or written
programs that compose perception and control [45, 46], and hierarchical systems pair high-level language
reasoning with low-level action generation [47, 48]. In 2026 such agents became competitive with end-to-

Harness effects are large. With the same planner and primitives, one study reports that writing code instead
of calling tools raises success from 63.1% to 71.7% [30]; a better harness lets a weaker model beat a stronger
one [59]; and outside robotics the scaffold alone moves accuracy by up to 28 points within one model [60].
These studies usually compare agents with published entries trained under each entry’s own protocol. Simulated
agent evaluations, ours included, commonly pause the simulator while the model computes, which hides its
real-time cost [61], and frontier models controlling physical arms directly are not yet precise or efficient enough
to finish tasks within a practical action budget [62]. SO-101 Bench compares agents and learned policies on the
same episodes after training every learned policy on the same data and compute, ablates harness and model
separately, and runs the agent on the real robot.

Manipulation benchmarks and evaluation practice.  Simulated benchmarks for generalist policies [12, 13,
14, 53, 63] face saturation and train–test overlap. LIBERO instruction conditioning largely selects among
memorized tasks [16]; policies above 90% there fall below 30%, or to zero, under modest perturbations [64, 65];
and an audit of five suites finds shortcut solvability, state-of-the-art gains not established as statistically significant,
creeping overfitting and dependence on the training-data source [25]. Responses include generalization suites [66,
63], capability suites for memory of occluded objects [67] and spatial grounding [10]. Real-world evaluation
has moved to distributed pairwise comparison [68], autonomous evaluation cells [69], and statistical methods
that separate policies with few trials [11, 70]. SO-101 Bench adopts several of these lessons: it separates unseen
instances from unseen classes and keeps part of the latter private, fine-tunes every policy on the same seen-object
data under one compute budget, selects checkpoints on a separate validation set, and reports confidence intervals
over 916 episodes. It also scores two spatial skills that, to our knowledge, few benchmarks test in closed loop:
placing an object between two referents, and rotating a grasped object to fit (PLAN).

3  SO-101 Bench

SO-101 Bench evaluates language-conditioned tabletop manipulation with a single SO-101 arm [1].  It is
designed to test whether a policy can turn semantic understanding into precise physical execution: identifying
the right object among distractors, grasping objects of unfamiliar geometry, and placing them under (often
precise) spatial constraints. Every component below is shared by all evaluated policies.


3.1 Tasks

The benchmark comprises four language-conditioned tasks (Fig. 2), scored as five task families.

       • Place each object in the plastic bin. The pure grasping task: the policy must identify, grasp, transport
       and deposit every object on the table. The bin moves between episodes. We evaluate a 1-object and a
        4-object condition as separate families.

       • Place [object 1] next to [object 2]. The policy must place the target close to a referent without
        disturbing other objects, adding semantic grounding and basic spatial placement.

       • Place [object 1] between [object 2] and [object 3]. The target must end centred between two referents,
       which makes the task sensitive to object extent, orientation and fine placement; it is the most demanding
         task.

       • Move [object 1] [direction]. The policy must push or carry the target along a straight path in a
      commanded direction until it reaches the boundary formed by the next object in its way.

The bin task stresses grounding, grasp strategy and grasp precision; the three spatial tasks additionally require
relational grounding, spatial reasoning, fine-grained placement and robustness to partial occlusion. To keep
language grounding nontrivial, distractors of the same class or colour are included so that class identity alone is
insufficient, and colour words are omitted from instructions unless necessary (i.e when two objects of the same
class are on the table).

instance does not), and unseen class (47 objects of entirely novel classes). The splits separate transfer across
instances from transfer across categories. Objects were chosen to maximize diversity of geometry and of
domain (e.g. office, kitchen, sports, toys), with priority on irregular shapes. Every object was verified through
teleoperation to be graspable by the SO-101, so that failures reflect the policy rather than the hardware. Of the
unseen-class objects, 37 are kept private to prevent test-set leakage.

All objects were created using the image-to-3D tools in 3D AI Studio [71]. The ∼60 physical objects were
reconstructed from photographs of the real items and their simulated appearance and physical properties were
tuned to match them; the remaining objects were generated from internet or AI-generated images and passed
through the same pipeline (Appendix E). All simulated objects are rigid bodies.


3.3  Digital Twin

All evaluation runs in a digital twin of the original real-world setup, built in Isaac Lab [26] from a scan of the
room and the object assets of Sec. 3.2. Physics runs at 240 Hz and the policy acts at 30 Hz. Policies observe
an overhead camera and a wrist camera, both at 640 × 480, and the arm’s joint positions. The twin includes
22 background environments: 18 are used in training and in the varied evaluation episodes, and 4 are held out
(Appendix F). The robot is rendered in one of 6 training colours or one of 4 held-out colours. The real arm’s
joint calibration is aligned to the simulated kinematics so that the same policy weights can run in both domains
(Sec. 5).


3.4  Scoring

Episodes are scored automatically from simulator state. Positions are measured in the tabletop plane from where
objects rest at the start of the episode. A success condition must hold continuously for 5 s; a failure condition
ends the episode once it has held for 5 s, so briefly undoing a mistake is allowed. The robot is considered to
touch an object when any link presses on it with more than 0.05 N. Episodes time out after 30 s (75 s for 4-object
bins).

3.5  Training Data

All learned policies are fine-tuned on so101_bench_sim: 3,629 teleoperated episodes (18.5 h at 30 fps) recorded
in the digital twin using seen objects only. It contains 1,892 bin episodes (including bin instructions that name a
single target among other objects), 1,150 next-to and between episodes, and 587 move episodes; 3,004 episodes
have four objects on the table. Most episodes are rendered with randomized lighting, camera intrinsics and
extrinsics, background and robot colour; the canonical setup remains in the training distribution. A variant,
so101_bench_sim_WM, adds the episode’s initial overhead and wrist frames for policies that accept them.
We also release so101_bench_real, approximately 4,400 real-robot teleoperated episodes (∼20 h) across
approximately 35 objects.


3.6 Primary Evaluation

The primary evaluation contains 916 scored episodes spanning the 15 task-family × split cells, with every object
appearing in each family it supports. Feasibility (spacing between objects) is checked for every layout so that a
poor arrangement cannot make success impossible. About half the episodes use the canonical appearance and
half vary the background and robot colour. We report the benchmark score, the mean success rate over the 15
cells, with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval that resamples episodes within cells. Three overlapping subsets
probe specific capabilities: ROBUST (178 episodes with held-out backgrounds and robot colours), PLAN (48
episodes in which the grasped object must be rotated to fit into a tight space), and MEM (51 episodes in which
the policy must remember the position and 3D footprint of an object that becomes occluded). Figure 4 shows a
successful example of each.

                                            84  Real-Only vs. Sim-Only Policy Correspondence

Before measuring sim2real transfer (Sec. 5), we ask a coarser question: does the digital twin reproduce the
difficulty structure of the real benchmark? If a policy trained in simulation and evaluated in the twin finds the
same tasks, splits and failure modes hard as a policy trained and evaluated in the real world, the twin is a useful
proxy for real-world evaluation even before any weights cross domains.

Setup. We fine-tune two GR00T N1.6-3B policies [72, 74] independently: a real-only policy on real tele-
operated demonstrations (so101_bench_real), evaluated on the physical SO-101, and a sim-only policy on
demonstrations collected in the digital twin (a subset of so101_bench_sim containing 3D scanned objects
from so101_bench_real, with 50% of the data volume of so101_bench_real), evaluated in simulation. We
compare them on 906 episodes matched across domains by task, instruction, ordered object set and object split.
Object poses are not identical across domains, so individual episodes are not exact replicas; the primary com-
parison is therefore at the level of the 15 task × split conditions and of failure composition, with episode-level
agreement reported as a secondary measure. Real-world outcomes and failure types were labelled by hand;
simulated failures were labelled the same way and both were mapped to three categories, semantic (wrong object
or referent(s)), grasping (grasp, lift or release failed) and placement (correct object handled, imprecise/incorrect
placement).

Difficulty is preserved across conditions.  The sim-only policy succeeds on 45% (409/906) of episodes and
the real-only policy on 61% (552/906), a gap of −15.8 pp (95% CI [−19.9, −11.8]). Despite this offset, the two
systems order the 15 conditions similarly: Pearson r = 0.86 [0.71, 0.91] and Spearman ρ = 0.74 [0.52, 0.91]
across cells (Fig. 5a). In both domains success is highest on the 1-object bin and seen objects and falls with task
difficulty and object novelty, with the 4-object bin and the between task hardest on unseen classes.

Failure modes are preserved.  The composition of failures on the spatial tasks follows the same trend in
both domains (Fig. 5b). On seen objects most failures are placement errors (69% real, 62% sim; total variation
distance 0.07); on unseen classes most are semantic or grasping errors (74% real, 93% sim). Across all splits the
two failure mixes differ by a total variation distance of 0.13. On the 4-object bin, the real-only policy bins 67%
of objects and the sim-only policy 47%; per-episode progress is weakly correlated across domains, likely due to
the small size of the sim dataset for this experiments (Spearman ρ = 0.35; Fig. 5c).

Episode-level agreement is moderate.  Paired episodes have the same outcome 66% of the time (MCC 0.36),
and where both failed the failure type matches in 47% of cases (Cohen’s κ = 0.17). This is expected given
differeing training dataset scales, initial poses and stochastic policies, and is why we emphasize condition-level
correspondence. Full results are in Appendix A.

Overall, because the two policies differ in training data as well as in evaluation domain, this experiment cannot
attribute the absolute gap to the simulator; the lower sim success reflects both policies and domains together.
What it does show is that the twin reproduces which conditions are hard and why policies fail there. Section 5
isolates the simulator by running identical weights (with sim training only) in both domains.


5  Sim2Real with No Real Data

A simulated benchmark is only useful if it tells us which policies are better in the real world. We test this
directly: five policies that never saw real data from our setup are evaluated, with identical weights, both in the

Abstract
The article describes the measurement of unidirectional pose accuracy and repeatability of a collaborative robot. The
objective of the measurements is to investigate and evaluate unidirectional accuracy of the six-axis collaborative robot
UR5 of the company Universal Robots. The measurement methodology was based on outlining an imaginary ISO cube
placed in the robot’s workspace, in which the robot’s tool centre point (TCP) attained five measurement points in thirty
measurement cycles. A video camera and six linear incremental sensors with six evaluation units were used for the mea-
surement. The measured values are presented and applied according to the ISO 9283 standard. On the basis of the mea-
surement, we verified technical specifications of unidirectional pose accuracy and repeatability of the robotic arm UR5
specified by its producer.


Keywords
Unidirectional pose accuracy, unidirectional pose repeatability, measuring cube, collaborative robot UR5, programming

## 1. sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000020)

               Kinematic Analysis and Integration of Vision
               Algorithms for a Mobile Manipulator Employed
                        Inside a Self-Driving Laboratory

                     Shifa Sulaiman1*, Tobias Busk Jensen1, Stefan Hein Bengtson2,
                                     Simon Bøgh1

                  1*Department of Electronic Systems, Aalborg University, Fredrik Bajers
                           Vej 7, Aalborg, 9220, North Denmark Region, Denmark.2025                  2Department of Architecture and Media Technology, Aalborg University,
Oct                Rendsburggade 14, City, 9000, North Denmark Region, Denmark.
21                   *Corresponding author(s). E-mail(s): ssajmech@gmail.com;
                     Contributing authors: tobjen21@student.aau.dk; shbe@create.aau.dk;
                                               sibo@es.aau.dk;



                                                  Abstract[cs.RO]                   Recent advances in robotics and autonomous systems have broadened the use
                              of robots in laboratory settings, including automated synthesis, scalable reac-
                            tion workflows, and collaborative tasks in self-driving laboratories (SDLs). This
                         paper presents a comprehensive development of a mobile manipulator designed to
                               assist human operators in such autonomous lab environments. Kinematic mod-
                              eling of the manipulator is carried out based on the Denavit–Hartenberg (DH)
                          convention and inverse kinematics solution is determined to enable precise and
                          adaptive manipulation capabilities. A key focus of this research is enhancing the
                          manipulator’s ability to reliably grasp textured objects as a critical component of
                       autonomous handling tasks. Advanced vision-based algorithms are implemented
                           to perform real-time object detection and pose estimation, guiding the manip-
                            ulator in dynamic grasping and following tasks. In this work, we integrate a
                             vision method that combines feature-based detection with homography-driven
                         pose estimation, leveraging depth information to represent an object’s pose as
                        a 2D planar projection within 3D space. This adaptive capability enables the

Autonomous robotic systems are reshaping research workflows by enabling scalable,
efficient, and safe operations in laboratory environments [1]. Within this shift, manipu-
lators mounted on mobile platforms [2], [3] have emerged as dynamic agents capable of
performing tasks like sample transport, equipment handling, and autonomous exper-
imentation. A cornerstone of these capabilities lies in reliable object tracking and
grasping, particularly when dealing with fragile or hazardous materials. To perform
these tasks with precision, vision-based object detection and pose estimation have
become central tools in robotics, allowing for real-time perception and adaptive motion
planning. Leveraging color and depth information, robots in self-driving laboratories
can interact with diverse objects, adjusting dynamically to changes in shape, texture,
and environmental conditions.

like lighting variability, occlusion, and clutter introduce complexity to object recogni-
tion and manipulation. Overcoming these challenges requires a synergistic framework
that combines mechanical modeling, control stability, and perceptual accuracy. In
this work, we propose a comprehensive system that integrates kinematic model of a
manipulator with real-time perception to enhance grasping reliability in self-driving
chemical laboratories. The mobile manipulator is developed to follow and grasp tex-
tured objects, supporting autonomous workflows and minimizing human intervention.

• Complete system integration: Developed a kinematic analysis framework for a
  mobile manipulator tailored to autonomous chemical laboratories, enabling seam-

  perception modules.
• Simulation and Real-World Performance Assessment  : Validated system
  performance via simulation and real-world experiments, reporting quantitative met-
   rics such as pose estimation error and grasping success rate to demonstrate feasibility
  and reliability.

   Despite substantial progress, object identification and pose recovery remain chal-
lenging in real-world laboratory environments due to variability in object shape,
texture, and appearance. These challenges are further exacerbated by occlusions, clut-
tered scenes, inconsistent lighting, and background interference, all of which degrade
the reliability of recognition algorithms. To address these issues, we updated a vision
pipeline [4] that integrates feature-based detection with homography-driven pose esti-
mation, augmented by depth sensing. This method enables robust 2D planar projection

where autonomous robotic systems continuously operate without human intervention,
leveraging real-time object detection and pose estimation techniques. The self-driving
laboratory provides a dynamic environment for validating adaptability and precision
in robotic grasping tasks, ensuring that robots can efficiently navigate, recognize, and
manipulate objects under varied conditions. By utilizing RGB and depth data within
this automated setting, we enhance robotic perception and interaction to follow a
textured object and facilitating reliable grasping.

traditional methods struggled with scale variation and complex backgrounds.

nique used for detecting and describing local features in images. It enables reliable

pose estimation enables tasks like grasping, navigation, and interaction with objects in

perception, enabling machines to understand and interact with their environment in
